Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo: Portugal boss Jorge Jesus responds to criticism from Ronaldo's mother
Sports.text:
Jorge Jesus has responded to claims by Cristiano Ronaldo's mother, Dolores Aveiro, that her son had been "deceived" by the Portugal manager.

Ronaldo, 41, retired from international football on 5 November, ending a career with his country during which he won 234 caps and scored 146 goals.

But his retirement also came less than a month after he had been given a 30-day suspension and fined £215 for walking out of the Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start the Nations League match against Denmark.

Portugal played their first game since Ronaldo's announcement against the Danes on Saturday, losing 4-1 at home.

While attending a Sporting event on Monday, Aveiro was asked about Ronaldo's national team retirement, and said:, external "Of course he was sad.

"They deceived him. And I'm sad, too. The defeat [against Denmark] was well-deserved. I was actually glad."

Before Portugal's Nations League game against Wales in Cardiff on Tuesday (19:45 GMT), Jesus was asked for his thoughts on Aveiro's comments.

"Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo's mother?" he said.

"She is a lady I greatly respect - she suffered a lot to raise her children."

Asked if the debate about Ronaldo's international retirement would end, Jesus added: "I don't know when it's going to stop.

"If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer."

Sports.title: Has James Trafford replaced Jordan Pickford as England No 1?
Sports.text:
It was some night for James Trafford.

As he was mobbed by his England team-mates for a late double save that secured a memorable 3-2 win against world champions Spain, the debate that followed about who the country's number one is was inevitable.

The Leeds keeper was given his chance to show England boss Thomas Tuchel what he could do again - and he absolutely took it.

On his fifth England cap the 24-year-old enjoyed a magnificent performance in Madrid as his side handed the hosts their first loss in 43 matches.

Trafford made four key saves in the final 12 minutes of the game, including an incredible double stop to first deny a Lamine Yamal curler and then dive again to his right to keep out Fermin Lopez from close range.

Last week Tuchel had made it clear that Everton goalkeeper Jordan Pickford was his number one.

But after full-time in Spain Tuchel told ITV Sport "there's no number one" and Trafford had "a brilliant match".

So, following his performance on Sunday night, is Trafford now likely to oust Pickford as England's go-to goalkeeper?

Despite being just 24 years old Trafford has already been England's most expensive goalkeeper by transfer fee... twice.

Trafford returned to his boyhood Manchester City from Burnley for a £31m fee in 2025 and then left the Etihad for Leeds for £45m this summer - having been limited to being Pep Guardiola's 'cup goalkeeper'.

Given the downturn in form of their current goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, many City fans may well be wishing Trafford had stayed. Their loss is Leeds' - and maybe England's - gain.

At Leeds he has found his form and this season ranks first among the 52 goalkeepers who have played at least 10 games in Europe's big five leagues by save percentage (81.4%).

He has made five appearances for England, all of them in 2026, and has rotated with Pickford across the Three Lions' five matches since the World Cup.

Pickford has started against Czech Republic and Croatia twice whereas Trafford has played against Czech Republic and started both England's matches with Spain, home and away.

After England's win in Madrid, which was the first time Spain had lost in the city in 39 years, Trafford's double-save was praised by his Three Lions team-mate Declan Rice.

"Everything happened so quick so for him to make two in the space of two seconds is massive," he told ITV. "A massive night for him."

Spain manager Luis de la Fuente agreed. He said: "We did generate some chances but England's goalkeeper has produced a fantastic performance and stopped two or three potential goals in the last 10 or 15 minutes."

After the double-save several England players ran over to celebrate with Trafford.

And on Tuchel's decision to rotate between his two keepers former Manchester United captain Roy Keane told ITV: "I think it's smart management.

"This is the perfect time for Trafford to come in, against top players, and show what he's capable of doing."

Social media has been full of the 'England number one' debate since, with many suggesting this was a moment that marked the changing of the guard.

Could Tuchel really now not start with Trafford for England's Nations League quarter-finals? Only time will tell.

What about Pickford though? England's undisputed first choice for almost 10 years has rarely let his country down.

The 32-year-old has won 94 caps for England since making his debut in a 0-0 draw with Germany in 2017 and during his time as number one England have reached two World Cup semi-finals and two Euros finals.

According to Opta stats, Pickford has only made two errors leading to goals across his England career, with 46 clean sheets and a 74.3% save ratio.

And since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.

"We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that," said former England number one goalkeeper Paul Robinson to BBC Sport before England's win against Spain,

"It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period.

"This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much.

"I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis any time soon, irrespective of the next selection."

This isn't a debate that is going away any time soon. But having two goalkeepers genuinely competing for that number one shirt can only be to England's benefit.

Sports.title: Sebastien Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Andy Robertson
Sports.text:
Angry captain Andy Robertson says Scotland do not have time to turn things around after a brutal 4-0 defeat by Switzerland consigned them to a third-place finish in their Nations League group.

Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli - appointed as Steve Clarke's successor in August - has consistently stressed the need for patience as he tries to implement a more attack-minded style.

However, the Belgian has won just two of his first six matches in charge, both against North Macedonia, and conceded 10 goals in that time.

They collapsed worryingly easily in St Gallen against a much-changed Swiss outfit on Monday after a promising start, Bologna midfielder Lewis Ferguson putting through his own goal and early intensity gave way to indecision.

The Swiss struck twice in the early minutes of the second half to make it 3-0 and Zeki Amdouni made it four late on.

"First half, I thought we were in the game, we lost a stupid goal, but I thought we had chances and could have been 2-1 at half time," a frustrated Robertson said, on the night he surpassed Kenny Dalglish as his country's most capped men's player.

"By the time you get to 50 minutes and you're 3-0 down, that can't happen in international football.

"It is a really tough night for us. I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it.

"These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."

This was meant to be a special occasion for Robertson, but it was usurped by the debate over Pocognoli's future.

Just six games into his tenure, there are serious questions being asked over whether the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco coach is capable of delivering on his promise of making Scotland easier on the eye, while delivering positive results.

Tottenham Hotspur left-back Robertson was not the only player to deliver a scathing assessment.

When asked if Scotland were on the right path, John McGinn replied: "Well, obviously the trajectory of the results means it's impossible for me to say yes."

Fellow midfielder Billy Gilmour added: "As a team we know we need to show passion and fight. We've not quite done that tonight."

Supporters are already frustrated at Pocognoli's 3-5-2 formation as they see wingers sidelined or - in the case of Ben Gannon-Doak - shoehorned into an unfamiliar wing-back role.

One man familiar with the difficulties of being the Scotland manager is former boss Craig Levein, who believes the Belgian needs to take a leaf out of his predecessor's book.

"Pocognoli is picking up where Clarke left off," Levein said on BBC Scotland. "In that situation, you need to get off to a good start. That's what the players are looking for - that you're going to make them better.

"I'd be thinking 'we need to stop losing goals'. We haven't got a potent threat, so how do we get results? As Steve recognised, you need to be hard to beat."

In contrast to his deflated players, Pocognoli put on a brave face post-match and insists he sees positive signs after his first two camps.

"The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game," he said.

"We played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments, and we faced Switzerland with different shapes and adapted well from the first minute. We conceded from maybe one of the first chances they had.

"At the end, it's a bad feeling, the score, but I think that the players try to do their best and create moments that we want to see."

Again Pocognoli called for patience and the time which Robertson says Scotland do not have.

"The more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things," the head coach said. "We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."

But whatever Pocognoli's selling, former Scotland winger Pat Nevin isn't buying.

"If I'm ever in trouble and I need a PR man, I'm getting him because he's absolutely good at it," he said on Sportsound.

"He's certainly a glass-half-full person. You can talk away any moment and say it's just a moment, but it's four moments, five moments, six moments.

"A really horrible thing in that situation is that if I am running the SFA, I'd be asking the players what they think and just saying 'tell us the truth... are you backing us?'

"If a couple of the main ones say 'we're not sure of the decision-making' then I think it's got to that stage."

Fraser: Utter shambles. Embarassing. How can players who play for so called "big" clubs look like they've never seen a football before when they put on a Scotland shirt?

Matt: Six games. Six poor results. Our ranking will tank. And all Clarke's good work will be undone. It's time to admit Mulholland got it wrong. Sometimes you don't need data and metrics to see the simple solution. Poco no more.

Shirleyanne: All these comments about how rubbish we are I would like to know if they are the same people who when we play well are getting in touch praising the team?? The manager needs time, the players need time too.. Yes it's not been great but come on give them a chance and get behind them instead of moaning..

Grant: Pocognoli is the new Russell Martin, talks a good game but is actually clueless and too stubborn to admit his tactics are dire. I did say be careful what you wish for when the gaffer quit in June and this will only end one way so might as well get it done well before March. Someone should call Steve Clarke.

Brett: When you have limited resources like Scotland, you have to utilise them to good effect - take a look at what Michael O'Neil is doing with Northern Ireland, he is getting results. And you can say that Scotland has a better pool of players to choose from than Northern Ireland does, so...

Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli - appointed as Steve Clarke's successor in August - has consistently stressed the need for...

Sports.title: Shoe Prices Hit a Record High Amid Inflation and Increased Tariffs
Sports.text:
Americans are paying more for sneakers, boots and high heels, another sign of how inflationary pressures have spread to nearly every aspect of consumer spending.

The war in Iran has driven up the price of oil, which has raised the price of gas, groceries and other goods transported by ship and truck. The surge in energy prices has affected the footwear industry too, as the some of the materials used to make shoes are synthetic byproducts of petroleum and thus more expensive.

Increased production costs combined with higher tariffs on products manufactured in Asia pushed shoe prices up 2.1 percent in the United States in October to their highest level, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The figure from the same period last year is missing because of a federal shutdown.

Still, there’s little sign that prices will fall soon. “We expect to see record footwear prices for the full year,” said Gary Raines, the chief economist of the Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America, a trade association. “That is strongly influenced by those average duties prepared on footwear that have been trending higher over the last year and a half.”

Historically, footwear price inflation has averaged 0.35 percent every six months from 2000 through June 2026. In the first half of this year, it rose 2.3 percent, the biggest semiannual jump since pandemic-related supply chain problems upended shoe production four years ago.

Shoe companies have worked to keep prices steady on their most popular items, such as Nike Air Force 1s and Crocs classic clogs, but have turned to incremental price increases on less vital products.

But even some of the most prominent shoe lines have increased prices. This year, Deckers Brands, the owner of Ugg, raised the price of its classic sheepskin boot 2.6 percent to $195 and said its Hoka running shoe brand would see some price increases this fall.

Footwear executives have said throughout the year that their businesses have been pinched by higher costs of materials such as leather and textiles. Andrew Rees, the chief executive of Crocs, said in April that its resin clogs, made from a proprietary foam, faced cost pressure as disruptions from the war in Iran sent oil prices skyrocketing.

Top executives from Adidas, Steve Madden and Birkenstock have each said that higher freight costs, brought on by those high oil prices, have affected their businesses.

Birkenstock said it had raised some prices as it pushed costs on to consumers. Ivica Krolo, the chief financial officer of Birkenstock, suggested on a conference call with analysts and investors in August that price-conscious shoppers traded down to the brand’s cheaper offerings.

“Our pricing decisions are made with the goal of passing through inflation and protecting gross margin,” Mr. Krolo said. “Something that we do very consistently.”

American consumers have kept spending this year even as they struggle with higher costs of living, but they are starting to pull back. In September, U.S. retail sales rose just 0.8 percent, down from a 1.3 percent gain in the previous month. Shoppers are expected to prioritize value in their purchases as retailers enter the crucial holiday season.

“The consumer keeps showing up,” Matt Priest, the chief executive of the Footwear Distributors group, said of the retail landscape. “But we don’t know how long that will last.”

Since President Trump returned to the White House, many of the world’s largest footwear brands, including Nike, Adidas, Skechers, Puma and Crocs, have pushed the administration to lower tariffs and alleviate pressure on their margins. In a letter sent to Mr. Trump last year, they said that the new tariffs presented an “existential threat” to the industry and asked him to consider an exemption.

The industry got a reprieve in February when the Supreme Court ruled that Mr. Trump was not authorized to unilaterally impose tariffs, but new duties under a different statute took effect in July.

The world’s largest shoe exporters are China, India, Vietnam, Indonesia and Bangladesh, and the United States has assigned each of these countries additional tariffs on top of duties already applied to footwear.

The Trump administration also left footwear out of its latest rounds of tariff exclusions, which have included categories such as wind turbines and commercial aircraft.

In July, the American Apparel and Footwear Association, an industry trade group with members that include Adidas and Steve Madden, sent a letter to the U.S. trade representative’s office that requested a list of footwear and other goods be considered for lower tariff treatment.

“Tariff relief broadly benefits U.S. workers in our industry,” Beth Hughes, the group’s vice president of trade and customs policy, wrote in the letter. “U.S. consumers stand to benefit since tariff costs ultimately make their way to the final consumer.”

Gaming_Tech.title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
Gaming_Tech.text:
After 13 years of waiting, some GTA 6 fans are taking extra steps to play the game - from booking time off work, buying a console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.

Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates, external GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn (£894m) from 12 million pre-orders - although Rockstar has not confirmed this.

Despite the option to preload the 212GB game, Jennifer Holmes, chief executive of the London Internet Exchange, said several UK internet providers including BT and Virgin Media had "increased capacity in anticipation of higher demand" ahead of launch.

But for some fans, simply having the game ready to play is not enough.

Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.

When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding, external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.

Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing , externaltaking several days off to play.

GTA 6 is no exception, but it appears to characteristically be taking things to a whole new level.

For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.

It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.

According to the HR firm, one person put "new GTA is coming out! I will be spending a week on the sofa in my pants!" as the reason for their leave request, while another said: "play the new GTA - I've waited a billion years".

A third said in their request: "GTA Release - I'll put my notice in if this is denied."

The company added it had no way of tracking if the requests had actually been approved by employers.

Some places have even decided to lean into the trend by offering incentives around the game – including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.

It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.

"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.

"There are 130 soldiers eligible within the battalion, and 20 have selected this incentive as part of their reenlistment," she said at the time.

Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.

This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.

According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.

Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.

"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.

"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.

It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.

GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither has Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from analyst firm Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".

Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.

Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.

"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.

A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.

Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.

Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.

"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.

"The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."

After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter what the cost or extra effort.

Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates, external GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn...

Gaming_Tech.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
Gaming_Tech.text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.

In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.

Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".

Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.

But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.

Gaming_Tech.title: Nvidia dismisses campaign to bring back Jensen Huang as Trump backs effort
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.

Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.

But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.

The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.

Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.

The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".

Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.

The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.

The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.

The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.

Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.

He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".

In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad.

The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.

Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.

But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.

But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external

"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."

But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".

Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.

Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".

Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk...

Gaming_Tech.title: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
Gaming_Tech.text:
Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services.

Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related".

Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening.

The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage, a network failure that grounded all US flights, and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage".

Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.

Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.

Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".

The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.

The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.

Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.

Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.

US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.

Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.

Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.

As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.

Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".

That issue resolved within a few hours.

The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.

The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.

The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), but comes as other industries report different outages around the US.

On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues.

The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.

Additional reporting by Max Matza.

Gaming_Tech.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
Gaming_Tech.text:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director of Megaspeed near the end of 2023, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS but it said she was still "practically in control" of the company.

Alice Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.

Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang had agreed to testify before the House Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the Foreign Affairs and the Intelligence committees.

The committees had threatened to issue subpoenas to Jensen Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.

Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued.

Jensen Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.

Moolenaar said: "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls."

Separately, a group of tech leaders including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive.

A representative forJensen Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded.

The BBC understands that the likelihood of him being reinstated is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing.

The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday, 17 November.

On Friday, Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by fellow cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well...

Gaming_Tech.title: Landeed, Fractal Analytics: The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
Gaming_Tech.text:
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.

Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.

Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.

Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.

He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.

"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.

These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.

The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.

Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.

Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.

An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.

With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.

The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.

Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.

Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.

Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.

It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.

On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.

"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.

In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.

The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.

It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.

This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.

Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.

"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.

"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."

Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.

"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.

"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.

The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.

Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.

Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.

"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.

From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.

"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.

"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.

Gaming_Tech.title: GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty after release from secure hospital
Gaming_Tech.text:
A hacker has pleaded guilty to a string of online crimes, including trying to extort the makers of Grand Theft Auto 6 after stealing dozens of unfinished clips of the game.

21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, carried out the hack in 2022, and was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

On Monday, Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

Kurtaj breached Rockstar Games in 2022 whilst he was on bail for multiple other hacking offences and under police protection.

He was being housed in a Travelodge in Bicester to protect him from rival hackers who threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.

With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.

He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

The company refused to cooperate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.

Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.79m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.

The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.

At the time, doctors deemed Kurtaj unfit to stand in a traditional trial due to the severity of his autism, so instead he was given what is known as a trial of the facts.

The jury was asked to determine whether or not he committed the alleged acts - not if he did so with criminal intent.

In December 2023 the court ruled that he would remain at a secure hospital for life unless doctors deem him no longer a danger.

A routine assessment late last year deemed that he was now fit to stand a criminal trial which was scheduled to take place at Woolwich Crown Court.

But Kurtaj pleaded guilty to all offences.

He sat in the dock with short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt but no tie.

The now 21-year-old blinked frequently during the hearing and stood to confirm his name, and pled guilty to all counts with no visible emotion.

In the 2023 original trial, another Lapsus$ member, who was 17, was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court.

The 17-year-old, who could not be named at the time due to his age, was sentenced to an 18-month Youth Rehabilitation Order, including intense supervision and a ban on using VPNs online.

Earlier this year that same hacker, now named as Thalha Jubair, was jailed for five years and six months after continuing his cyber crime offences with another group known as Scattered Spider.

Amongst victims was Transport for London which was subjected to a disruptive cyber attack that caused around £39m of damage and caused chaos inside the firm.

Gaming_Tech.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
Gaming_Tech.text:
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.

The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".

Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.

The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

Gaming_Tech.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
Gaming_Tech.text:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta, which also runs WhatsApp and Instagram, 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech company.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.

The charge is related to a feature that suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. A preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery, according to the Italian regulator.

The regulator said it had taken into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact that the feature was "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation" in its decision.

Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law and the disproportionate level of the fine.

"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."

Last month, Meta was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

Gaming_Tech.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
Gaming_Tech.text:
Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption.

The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected.

The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.

Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent.

Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.

Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.

Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge.

In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected, as were some schools and police forces.

UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network.

In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.

In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.

Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.

In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.

The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.

Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill".

His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.

"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said.

"We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible."

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.

It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.

By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.

Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.

"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.

Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.

"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.

Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.

"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

Gaming_Tech.title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
Gaming_Tech.text:
After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.

The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.

And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment.

"We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.

Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?

Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.

The original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards.

Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase.

Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table.

"At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?"

Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car".

He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together".

The team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer.

But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book".

"At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds.

Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it".

"For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow.

"And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?"

Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt.

"We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way."

Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today.

Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald.

"It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US."

Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem.

Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA.

"It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says.

"Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole."

When GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time.

The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming.

"I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones.

MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round.

She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself.

As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life".

"It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving."

GTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue.

Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.

This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it.

The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game.

"Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald.

"It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time.

"It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in."

Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it?

"I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says.

"But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well."

Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful".

"It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic."

Gaming_Tech.title: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore
Gaming_Tech.text:
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.

For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.

With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.

But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.

Megaspeed is a case in point.

It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

The city-state has had some success in policing this.

It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.

They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.

In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.

The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.

Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.

But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.

Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.

In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.

Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.

Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.

In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.

Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.

Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.

On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".

China has also long rebuffed accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.

How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.

In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.

But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.

Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.

BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.

In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.

Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.

Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.

All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.

"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.

Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".

But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.

With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.

Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.

Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.

"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.

But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".

"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."

Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

Entertainment.title: James Bond: Robert Pattinson to replace Daniel Craig as 007
Entertainment.text:
Robert Pattinson, the British actor known for films such as Twilight and The Batman, has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

The announcement was made by Amazon MGM Studios in a social media post on Monday, with a picture showing Pattinson in character as 007.

The 40-year-old becomes the seventh actor to play the famous fictional spy and will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

In his statement, Pattinson said he was "deeply grateful" to the film's creative team "for their belief in me".

"To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement," he added. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Daniel Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

The next 007 film will be the first since long-term Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson stepped back and Amazon took creative control of the franchise, after acquiring the series' parent company MGM.

By the time the 26th Bond film is released, it will have been seven years since the last - 2021's No Time To Die - the biggest gap in the franchise's history.

Director Villeneuve is best known for films including the Dune trilogy, Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, while writer Knight is known for TV hits Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer and Locke.

Pattinson has already worked with Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3, where he stars as a new villain, Scytale. The film is released next month.

In a statement reacting to Pattinson's Bond casting, Villeneuve said: "Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond.

"He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

Pattinson's casting was also welcomed by Buckingham Palace, with a post on Instagram sharing the news and adding: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."

Australian actor George Lazenby, who played James Bond in the 1969 film On Her Majesty's Secret, posted a video on social media welcoming Pattinson to "the most exclusive club in the world".

"Remember to enjoy yourself... Let's see if you'll have 'this never happened to the other fella' moment," Lazenby said.

"All the best mate."

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

Craig appeared in five Bond movies in total, starting with 2006's Casino Royale, and spent 16 years as the secret agent created by author Ian Fleming.

In a statement, Fleming's estate said they were "delighted to welcome Robert Pattinson to the James Bond family".

The next film will mark a new era for the franchise. Amazon purchased MGM for $8.5bn in 2021, which included the rights to distribute James Bond.

Then in 2025, long-time Bond producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson agreed to sell creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM.

Before that, the franchise had been under the Broccoli family's control since 1962's Dr. No, when Sean Connery first starred as Bond.

The Broccoli family preserved the integrity of the character and brand for decades, resisting spin-offs and licensing that some industry experts now expect to see following Amazon's takeover.
