Entertainment.title: Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007
Entertainment.text:
Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.

He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.

At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role, but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.

His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.

Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.

He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with "appealing vulnerability, external".

Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama, he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance", external. It's one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year, along with The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.

Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.

His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.

"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008, external.

"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.

"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."

He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.

Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.

Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.

He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.

"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.

"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."

In 2010, Time included him in their list of 100 people who "most affect our world", external, saying perhaps prophetically that "we haven't seen a tenth of what he can do on screen".

After such mainstream success with the Twilight franchise, Pattinson was able to branch out.

He went on to work with several acclaimed independent film directors including David Cronenberg, starring in his film Cosmpopolis in 2012, as well as working with Werner Herzog in 2015's Queen of the Desert and The Lighthouse (2019), directed by Robert Eggers.

Pattinson told Screen Daily why he took the role in psychological horror film The Lighthouse, external, saying he told Eggers: "I just want to do something weird."

With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.

But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.

Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.

"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times, external.

"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.

"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."

Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

Entertainment.title: Grammys 2027: Raye leads with 11 nominations as Dolly Parton receives posthumous nods
Entertainment.text:
British singer Raye leads the charge at the forthcoming Grammy Awards with 11 nominations, while Dolly Parton has been recognised with three posthumous nods.

Raye is nominated for her latest Mercury-winning record This Album May Contain Hope and its lead single Where Is My Husband!, which is up for both song and record of the year.

Other nominees include Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Dean, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo, Miranda Lambert and Phoebe Bridgers.

Parton's two nominations, both in the best country duo/group performance category, come three months after the country music star died aged 80.

Parton is recognised for Butterfly, her collaboration with the Zac Brown Band, and Light of a Clear Blue Morning, alongside an all-star line-up including her goddaughter Miley Cyrus.

The late country star also received a nomination for best audio book, for her narration of Star of the Show: My Life on Stage.

The Grammy Awards 2027 will take place on Sunday 7 February in Los Angeles.

Madonna's album Confessions II, a sequel to 2005's Confessions on a Dancefloor, was absent from the "big four" categories - including album, record and song of the year.

That will be seen by many as the Grammys continuing their tradition of snubbing the US singer, but the album did make it into the best dance category.

Rosalía's nine nominations for her widely acclaimed album Lux come after her huge success at last week's Latin Grammy Awards.

Langley's seven nominations include song of the year for her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas, which this year became the longest-running number one single in the history of Billboard's Hot 100.

Entertainment.title: James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film
Entertainment.text:
When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"

Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.

"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.

British actor Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the next actor to play James Bond.

He shot to fame as Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and went on to star in Twilight.

Pattinson appeared opposite Kristen Stewart in the series of five films based on Stephenie Meyers' vampire novels.

He has gone on to star in other major films and franchises including The Batman and Christopher Nolan's recent adaptation of The Odyssey.

But Pattinson is also respected within the industry for his unusual choice of roles, often appearing in independent, arthouse and experimental films.

His other credits include The Lighthouse, Mickey 17, Life, The Drama, Good Time, Primetime, The Rover, Bel Ami, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.

The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."

He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."

Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight, known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.

Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.

He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.

"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."

With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.

It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version, external of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said, external he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.

Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Ian Fleming's original character and books.

Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, Christmas has come early for fans who have been waiting for years to find out who the next 007 will be.

In Robert Pattinson, producers have finally found their spy.

Entertainment.title: Emma Barnett: Host to leave Radio 4's Today and start new BBC show
Entertainment.text:
Radio 4 presenter Emma Barnett is set to leave the Today programme this week for a multiplatform new BBC show in the New Year.

Former Woman's Hour host Barnett has developed a "bold" new show, she says, which will launch in 2027 across BBC Sounds, BBC iPlayer and YouTube.

Her final day presenting Radio 4's flagship morning news and current affairs show will be on Wednesday 18 November.

"For the last nearly six years - it's been incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners," she said in a statement. "Having proudly hosted Woman's Hour and now the Today Programme - I've had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network."

She added: "But it's not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives."

Posting on Instagram, external, she said there would be more information on what her new show would be about soon.

"Watch this space and look ready. I am… More soon."

Barnett joined Today in May 2024, taking over from Martha Kearney to work alongside co-presenters Nick Robinson, Mishal Husain, Amol Rajan and Justin Webb. Husain and Rajan have since left.

Today programme editor Rebecca Keating said Barnett had brought "enormous energy" to Today, with "a keen focus" on listeners.

She noted how Barnett had a proven "track record of telling stories of personal hardship that influence public debate" but how she was "also equally at home interviewing British icons like Dame Judi Dench.

"We will miss her generous tea making and wish her every success in her new venture."

In August, Barnett, 41, revealed she had had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis, days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.

She returned to the Today programme explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".

Speaking on her BBC podcast, Ready to Talk with Emma Barnett, last year, she told listeners that finding out she was going through perimenopause at the age of 38 felt like she had been "mugged, robbed".

The broadcaster said it was the "first time in my life I haven't really wanted to be a woman - it's the first time I've thought, I'd really quite like to be a bloke".

Radio 4 controller Mohit Bakaya said he was "delighted she's staying with the BBC" and would "look forward to her new show."

Entertainment.title: Russell Brand prison message claiming innocence being investigated, No 10 says
Entertainment.text:
A message by Russell Brand to his followers in which he claimed innocence for his sexual offences was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is "completely unacceptable".

In a post on X, Norris wrote: "Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims.

"This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules."

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can be seen sitting on a sofa and is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

Relaying the message from her husband, Laura Brand said the comedian - who is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire - called prison staff "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

She said she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".

Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Speaking earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."

"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.

Victims' commissioner for London Andrea Simon said the claims will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma.

"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."

While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".

She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.

If Brand is found to have broken prison rules, possible punishments enforceable by prison governors can result in restrictions on social visits or loss of privileges such as access to additional time in the gym or loss of TV.

Governors can also impose proportionate restrictions on communications where justified.

This could include blocking specific phone numbers, increased monitoring of calls or restricting contact with individuals where necessary to protect victims or maintain prison security.

Meanwhile, there have been calls for a change in the law following Brand's conviction so that sexual relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal. The government says a discussion is to take place.

Mia Latter, who has alleged she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16, is among those campaigning for ministers to introduce a staggered age of consent.

She was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time. None of the women were complainants in his recent criminal trial.

Latter, who was known under the pseudonym "Alice" in the 2023 investigation, has now waived her right to anonymity.

In an interview with LBC on Monday, Latter said: "We don't want to criminalise anybody under the age of 18 [including] 16, 17-year-olds, 18-year-olds having sex with each other...

"I think healthy relationships are important, and they're important in helping you develop and grow."

But she said there should be an age "threshold" for the partners of 16 and 17 year-olds.

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, is urging a change in the law to prevent 16 year-olds from having a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and someone aged 17 from having a relationship with anyone older than 20.

She told BBC Breakfast that "predators know exactly what they are doing".

Asked about the issue on BBC Breakfast, the foreign secretary said: "I think the reason why it's right to have this debate is we've seen some of the very, very brave victims of Russell Brand come forward and say 'we think this needs looking at'".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said she is glad there is a conversation around staggering the age of consent but warned that it had "been quite complicated to actually implement" in some US states where it is used.

Trott said a suggestion that the age of consent should be raised to 18 is also a "conversation we need to have" but "probably isn't practical".

Anna Edmundson, director of policy & social change at the NSPCC charity, said: "We urgently need a review of what is and isn't working to ensure 16 and 17-year-olds are fully protected in law from this predatory behaviour.

"However, closing these gaps will only be part of the solution. We must question why adults have been able to exploit teenagers in plain sight for so long, and look at what further action is needed to help people recognise the signs of exploitation."

Any change in the law would only affect England and Wales as Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate legislative powers in relation to the age of consent, which is also currently set at 16 in both nations.

The Scottish Government said it had "no current plans" to change the age of consent, following the calls by campaigners, but any proposals would be considered.

Entertainment.title: Sir Tom Jones announces Wales gigs after cancelling shows
Entertainment.text:
Sir Tom Jones has announced two headline shows in Wales just weeks after he was forced to cancel or reschedule a number of tour dates due to illness.

The 86-year-old Welsh music icon's homecoming, as part of his Come Gather Round world tour, will see him perform at Cardiff Castle on 30 May, followed by a fully-seated show at Llangollen Pavilion in Denbighshire on 28 June.

Heather Small will feature as a special guest at the Cardiff show, while soul band Stone Foundation will also join the bill at both concerts.

It is a return to home soil for the legendary singer from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, who last performed in Wales in summer 2025.

Last month, Sir Tom was forced to cancel or reschedule shows in the US-leg of the world tour, due to "a bad case of flu".

He said at the time that he was "truly sorry" for the disappointment caused to fans, later adding he feared his life was "over" after being admitted to hospital.

Tickets for his Welsh gigs go on sale on 20 November, and the sets will feature tracks from his 2021 album Surrounded By Time, alongside fan favourites including It's Not Unusual, What's New Pussycat?, Delilah and Green, Green Grass of Home.

Nick Saunders, founder of promoter Depot Live, said: "Tom Jones is a true Welsh icon, so it's a real pleasure to welcome him back to Cardiff Castle.

"He's one of Wales' greatest-ever musical exports, and there's always a real sense of pride in seeing him perform on home soil."

Dave Danford, artistic director of the Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod, added: "His show here in 2024 was one of the most memorable evenings in the venue's history, and we've been trying to find a way to get him back here ever since."

Entertainment.title: Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison HMP Littlehey, his wife confirms
Entertainment.text:
Russell Brand has been transferred to a category C prison, his wife Laura has confirmed, in her first public comments since he was jailed.

On Monday, the comedian was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from category B HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.

Laura Brand returned to the couple's podcast on Sunday, saying that she had spoken to her husband in prison and he "is OK and is praying". Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

HMP Littlehey, a category C training prison, is one of the largest prisons in Europe for men convicted of sexual offences.

It held more than 1,200 prisoners as of January 2025, according to data from the Independent Monitoring Board.

Before Brand's move to the prison, a source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" at HMP Wandsworth and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival, with some slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. They added that there had also been some anger displayed about his crimes.

Staff at other prisons told the BBC Brand's fame, combined with the nature of his crimes, could make him a target for other inmates.

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can be seen sitting on a sofa in what looks like a conservatory. She is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

The couple had continued their YouTube podcast during Brand's trial. They often read snippets of the Bible and discussed religion.

On Sunday, Laura told their followers: "We trust his [God's] plan and everything he is doing just now, even though it's painful and obviously will take some getting used to."

During the show, Laura played an episode she said had been recorded before her husband was jailed.

It featured the couple singing to a recording of the American folk singer Woody Guthrie before praying together.

Towards the end of the podcast, Laura returned on her own to read a message from her husband, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences he had been jailed for.

He called staff at HMP Littlehey "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and he asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

Andrea Simon, the Victims' Commissioner for London, said the continued broadcast of Brand's podcast "is really problematic".

Simon told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the show "will certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape".

While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders like Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".

The commissioner added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.

Entertainment.title: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal against sexual assault conviction
Entertainment.text:
French film star Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexual assault, admitting that his behaviour towards women had often been offensive and offering a "deep and sincere" apology.

On the day that the appeal was due to start in a Paris court, the 77-year-old actor's unexpected mea culpa marks a dramatic reversal of his previous denials of sexual impropriety.

"Justice was pronounced. I was found guilty. I understand and bow to this conviction… I have therefore decided to abandon the appeal," he wrote.

It means he is now guilty in law of abusing two women during a film shoot in Paris five years ago, and his 18-month suspended prison term stands.

"Victory is ours, and we welcome it with head held high," said one of the two women, named only as Amélie, who was at the court.

"There is huge relief because the fight is over. The giant of film has fallen," said the other woman in the case, who is known in court by the false name Sarah.

In his statement, Depardieu appeared to have undergone a major shift from his earlier stance of unapologetic intransigence.

"For a long time on film shoots I hid myself behind provocation and smut. I thought that the remarks I made, and certain gestures that I made, were of no consequence.

"I see now that there is a border between impertinence and offence. Never, ever did I intend to hurt the women with whom I came into contact. But I see now that intention has no bearing on the hurt that people feel.

"Cases before the courts are damaging. Everything got out of hand… including my defence. Many people have suffered in this story. I have not the power to go back in time. I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that has disappeared."

The reference to his defence "getting out of hand" follows widespread criticism of the aggressive line taken by Depardieu's lawyer during the original trial in March last year.

Entertainment.title: Tourette's film I Swear wins three Scottish Baftas
Entertainment.text:
I Swear was the big winner at the Bafta Scotland awards on Sunday.

The film about Tourette syndrome campaigner John Davidson won Best Film, Best Director and Best Actor.

The condition causes involuntary vocal and physical tics and, in Davidson's case, coprolalia, which causes him to shout offensive and inappropriate phrases.

Davidson was at the centre of controversy when he attended the Bafta film awards earlier this year. His shouts, which included a racial slur, were heard in the hall during the event and broadcast in the BBC coverage of the event.

Davidson, from Galashiels, said he had been deeply affected by the experience but was determined to attend the awards in Glasgow, where I Swear was nominated in six categories.

" I didn't want to give people the impression I was hiding away," he said.

"So I spoke to Bafta Scotland and said 'how can we can make it easy, less stressful, and less complicated than it was in London?'".

The answer was to brief guests about Davidson's condition.

A Bafta Scotland staff member was with him during any interactions with members of the public.

Davidson, his family and friends, watched the awards via video link from a separate room in the Glasgow hotel where the ceremony took place.

Davidson said he hoped the film would raise awareness and increase understanding of the condition, which affects about 300,000 people in the UK.

I Swear's director, Kirk Jones, thanked the town of Galashiels and Tourette's groups in Scotland for supporting the film as he picked up the first of three awards.

He also paid tribute to John Davidson for sharing his story.

"I know it's been a long and difficult journey," he said. "Thank you for having the strength to continue that journey and for stressing the importance of acceptance and empathy at a time when the world desperately needs it."

He added: "My big hope was that it would help people understand those with Tourette's.

"What I didn't realise was that there's a much wider community of people with neurodiverse conditions who have connected with the film and feel for the first time there's a representation of a condition which is often hidden."

For Davidson, Sunday's wins are the celebration he was hoping for at the Baftas earlier this year.

"Tonight's not really about me, although it is my story," he said.

"It's about celebrating the actors and a beautiful film. I was blown away when I first saw it. I've never watched it since because it makes me cry.

"So I'm chuffed to bits that it's won tonight."

Entertainment.title: Shakespeare boss threatens to quit over Stratford to Birmingham move
Entertainment.text:
The director of the Shakespeare Institute has said he will resign if plans to move the centre from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham go ahead.

Professor Michael Dobson said he was "very unhappy" with the University of Birmingham's decision to relocate the postgraduate research institute from its historic home at Mason Croft to the university's Edgbaston campus in September 2027.

"Stratford has been the place where people come to dream of Shakespeare since the 18th Century," he said.

The Shakespeare Institute announced on Facebook on Friday that it had been informed it would leave Stratford after more than 75 years. The future of Mason Croft, along with its historic garden and playing fields, has not yet been confirmed.

The University of Birmingham said the move was "an academic decision" rather than a cost-cutting measure and insisted Shakespeare studies remained a priority.

It said the decision is about the Institute's "long-term future" and "current students, including research students, will be supported individually through the transition".

It added it would consult the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC), the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, local representatives and the wider community in the coming weeks.

However, Dobson rejected the university's characterisation of the decision.

"It affects academics, but it's not an academic decision in which anybody who works on Shakespeare at the University of Birmingham wishes to agree or go along with," he said.

"For 75 years Birmingham has been the only university in the world teaching and studying Shakespeare in Shakespeare's hometown," he said.

"That gives it enormous symbolic capital and has done wonders for the university's visibility and reputation in the humanities."

Dobson said Stratford was "the focus of the world's love of Shakespeare" and claimed the institute helped keep the town on the "intellectual and scholarly map" as well as its tourist and theatrical map.

The Shakespeare Institute, which celebrated its 75th anniversary in July, has worked with academics, writers and performers for decades, including Dame Judi Dench.

Meanwhile, a petition calling on the university to reverse its plans has been signed by thousands of people., external

The campaign urges the university to keep the Institute at Mason Croft, its Grade II listed home since 1951. It also calls for the publication of the rationale, financial figures and equality impact assessments behind the proposal.

Campaigners argue relocating the Institute would damage Stratford's cultural and academic standing and threaten postgraduate Shakespeare studies in a town closely linked to both William Shakespeare and the Royal Shakespeare Company.

The university said the Institute's library "will be kept together as a collection" and "none of it will be disposed" with plans for moving and housing the collection set out "shortly".

It added: "Mason Croft has been the Institute's home since 1951, and we are very mindful of its history.

"No decision has been taken on its future, and it remains the Institute's home for this academic year."

Entertainment.title: This City Is Ours actor reaches new heights in Liverpool drama
Entertainment.text:
With millions of viewers and a major role in a Bafta-nominated series, you might not expect Adam Abbou to know much about feeling self-conscious.

"When we were kids it wasn't so cool to be from Liverpool," the This City Is Ours actor says.

"I'd be in these rooms with people who were really posh and I always felt out of place."

The Liverpool-based BBC series has become a hit, with Abbou, who plays Freddie, stepping into a prominent role for its second season.

But it's not just the storylines on drugs, gangs and murders hooking audiences - it's the setting too, and the Scouse actors bringing it to life.

Created by Liverpudlian writer Stephen Butchard, This City Is Ours recruited heavily from Merseyside.

Lead actors James Nelson-Joyce, Jack McMullen and Mike Noble were all born in Liverpool, as was Abbou, who grew up in Anfield.

But like many young and aspiring actors, for a long time he thought where he came from could hold him back.

"I didn't see a lot of [Liverpudlian accents] on TV when I was a kid," the 23-year-old says.

As a result, acting "always felt really out of reach".

Abbou played the title role in a touring production of Billy Elliot the Musical in 2015, and has since appeared in dramas like Casualty, Time and Waterloo Road.

He says he wasn't expecting his latest gig, where he plays Freddie, gangster Banksey's son, to become so significant.

"If you would have asked me 10 years ago, I would have said you probably need to move to London," he says.

"So for me to be able to do a show like this in Liverpool, it just further proves that you can do it from anywhere."

Abbou is passionate about promoting working-class stories and actors from underprivileged backgrounds, who he says are "some of the hardest working kids you'll ever come across".

While This City Is Ours provided him with his big break, he says more needs to be done across the industry to open doors.

New research from the Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre, external published last week found representation of people from working-class backgrounds has fallen over the past five years, from 25% in 2021 to 21% now.

"I think it's a trust issue," Abbou says, with producers less willing to take risks on new talent.

"But if you give a working-class kid a chance they will run with it and they won't let you down."

From the reaction he's had locally, Abbou thinks the series has been a boost for Liverpool overall.

The reaction has been "quite crazy" in the city, he says, "but of course it would be because people love to see themselves and their accent reflected on TV and when it is, you almost feel like you know the person".

"It has truly been incredible to see the rise of the Scouse accent," he adds, crediting the Netflix series Adolescence, starring and co-created by Stephen Graham, with accelerating the change.

"Stephen Graham really was the one who started the wave for Scouse actors," he says.

"And then the likes of Jodie Comer and now you've got your Mike Nobles, your James Nelson-Joyces... and now your Adam Abbous.

"We're making waves for young Scouse talent."

As for what's next, Abbou says the series has helped push his career forward and he has some "exciting projects lined up" which he can't speak about just yet.

"I just want to do things that make me feel creatively fulfilled and mean something and have a voice."

- The last episode of The City Is Ours season two airs on BBC One at 21:00 GMT.

BreakingNewsTab.title: The young people caught up in Britain's Neets crisis
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The number of young people who are not in work, at school or in college is both an economic and moral crisis, a landmark report into the problem will say later.

The 241-page report, by ex-Labour minister Alan Milburn, will set out a raft of recommendations for the government to consider.

Ahead of its publication, four young people who are not in education, employment or training - those dubbed as "Neets" - tell us why they can't get a job and how the government could help them get one.

Michael, 19, who lives with his dad in the Wirral, says he dropped out of college and spent a year at home after his social anxiety "got really bad". It is "very easy" to fall out of the system, he says, if there is little support available.

Michael's story is not unique. There has been a large rise in anxiety and mental health problems in young people.

About one in five Neets have a mental health condition, according to 2025 data, external from the Department for Education (DfE) - more than double the rate in 2012.

Having signed up for Universal Credit, Michael was put in touch with the Merseyside Youth Association to help him find a job. He says mentors there have helped him improve his mental health, which led to him dropping out of college during his A-levels. He says that left him trapped inside his bedroom.

He says jobs in his area are scarce and those that do come up tend to go to older people with more experience. Michael says he is trapped in the cycle of not having the experience needed to build more.

"Everything is experience, experience, experience - that's the one thing that I always used to hear when going for jobs on my own without the help," he says.

We followed Michael for a day, meeting him after his 05:00 start for a work experience shift at a local supermarket that the Merseyside Youth Association helped him get.

Lots of Neets receive Universal Credit. For under-25s, the standard rate is £338.58 a month, external, which Michael gets. For some people who cannot work because of a health condition, disability or long-term illness, an additional £217.26 to £429.80 per month may be available.

Ahead of the publication of his full review, it was reported that Milburn would recommend young people should no longer be able to claim those additional health-related benefits, as part of a major overhaul of the welfare system.

Michael acknowledges some young people may be "taking advantage" of the benefits system, but says most "just want the money to get by so they can get a job".

More recently, he has been doing shifts at the Merseyside Youth Centre's on-site cafe to gain more much-needed experience. His hope is to be in a steady job earning money this time next year, with space to have his own art studio one day.

"From three months ago I'm a different person," he says. "I can do stuff, keep going."

Maariyah, a 22-year-old history and politics graduate, finished her university course last summer. Her dream is to work in museums.

However, she is currently unemployed and looking for any paid job after working a temporary six-month contract for a housing association earlier this year.

She says she spends hours each day in her local library - where she feels more able to focus than she can at home - submitting at least 20 tailored job applications a week.

Those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualifications are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods - however, an estimated one in 10 Neets are university graduates.

Maariyah says she is applying for roles in retail and restaurants, alongside unpaid work experience opportunities in the heritage sector.

But she says she has also been rejected for voluntary roles because they had too many applicants, or because she does not have enough experience. "I'm actively going out of my way to do unpaid work, only to get rejected from these positions," she says.

Not hearing back from employers "happens so often now that's it's like second nature", she says, adding that she finds it frustrating that many of her applications are likely to be screened by AI before a real person sees them.

On the day we meet, Maariyah heads to the job centre for her Universal Credit appointment after a library job application session. She says she has noticed an improvement in the support she gets there since she first received the benefit in 2025.

This time, she will be getting some mandatory hospitality training, which she says she is "really glad" to have.

She feels there is a growing sense of disillusionment among others her age. Being on benefits has become normalised because it is so hard to find a job, she adds.

It makes her feel that going to a good university, getting certain grades and doing extracurricular activities "doesn't make a difference in the end".

"I would like employers to give young people a chance to gain experience and take a chance on hard-working people who at the end of the day want a job so that they can contribute to our economy and contribute to their own lives."

Matthieu, 19, from Edgware in north-west London, is autistic and currently volunteers at a gardening club and a computer repair shop.

We meet him in Finsbury Park, where he is helping to mulch some newly planted trees. Working in nature is calming, he says.

He is looking for work with the support of the charity Ambitious About Autism and his mentor, Annie. He previously did a year-long supported internship with the Whittington hospital.

Matthieu says speaking to people face-to-face there helped his confidence and he enjoyed being part of the team. At his family home, Matthieu's mentor Annie tells us that not having maths and English GCSE qualifications is a barrier to finding employment.

Matthieu says he's more of a manual worker and wants to work in a factory, warehouse or doing deliveries, so that he can contribute financially for his family.

Alex, 20, from St Helens, has been looking for work for a year. She struggles with anxiety and is looking for roles as a cleaner or in retail. She also shares caring responsibilities for her mum with her other family members.

We meet her at Spear, an employment and mindset coaching programme. Alex says her dream is to work with animals. She says she had been studying Level 3 animal management at college before dropping out last year because of her mental health.

"I was so burnt out," she says. "I was struggling to get out of bed, I couldn't do anything. I was dragging myself to college. I was like, 'No, I need to have a break for a bit and try and figure out what to do after that'."

Building up her resilience is something she now works on with a mentor, as well as job applications.

Alex says she is applying for "anything and everything" and wants to get off benefits. She is also currently receiving Universal Credit, which she says is "all the money that I've got until I get a job and I'm earning more".

When asked what she thinks about potential benefits cuts for young people out of work, Alex says not being able to access benefits would "make life so much worse".

And she says trying to find work in a place like St Helens is harder, because many businesses in the town centre have either "gone or moved or shut down".

"Lots of people think, 'well, young people just don't want to work,'" she says. "But we do. We so desperately want to work. Places don't want to hire us."

Milburn has already said the system isn't working for everyone, and that serious action is needed to avoid young Neets becoming a "lost generation".

Additional reporting by Branwen Jeffreys and Kate McGough

BreakingNewsTab.title: Met Police missed opportunities stop predatory detective who ran rape unit, BBC finds
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Warning: Contains details of violence, coercion and sexual abuse - and strong language

The Metropolitan Police repeatedly missed opportunities to stop a predatory detective inspector from sexually exploiting women whose cases he investigated, including one who married him and later died in unexplained circumstances, BBC Panorama can reveal.

Warren Arter used his position - running a unit investigating sexual assaults in south-east London - to target women it was his job to protect.

Two women, speaking out for the first time, have told Panorama how Arter groomed them. One says he raped her.

In the case of his wife, Rebekah, he filmed her being sexually abused and distributed the footage. She died in Barbados two years ago, while on holiday with him. On Sunday, the BBC revealed how he lied about what happened on the Caribbean island.

There were multiple investigations into Arter while he was employed by the Met. Now the former detective who led one of them has told the BBC that senior bosses tried to interfere with his inquiries, despite him having found potential victims.

While Arter was suspended as a result of that investigation, he remained on full pay for seven years - before being sacked in 2023 for drug offences.

The following year, the Met - having learned of his wife's death in Barbados - arrested him on his return to the UK for sexual offences alleged by another woman.

Arter took his own life days later in HMP Wandsworth. Despite the evidence against him, the Met has not reviewed all the cases he handled.

In response to our investigation, the Metropolitan Police has for the first time publicly apologised to the women he abused. It said it was now working to examine Arter's electronic devices to identify if there are further victims and that it encouraged other women to come forward.

Panorama has uncovered several opportunities to stop Arter that were missed by the Met:

In 2010, medical staff found Arter alone with a woman in the toilets of a sexual assault referral centre hours after she had reported being raped. Despite the Met being told, this did not lead to an investigation

The Met received six corroborated intelligence reports into sexual misconduct by Arter between 2014 and 2018

The force failed to arrest Arter in 2024 after being told he had sent an illegal upskirting image, and only did so after Rebekah's death three months later

This last missed opportunity came after the Casey Review's conclusion that the Met was "institutionally misogynistic", as well as the convictions of rapist and murderer Wayne Couzens, and rapist David Carrick - both Met officers - and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley's promise to "lift the stone" and "tackle everything underneath it".

Panorama can now reveal that 21 potential victims of Arter were identified in an investigation by the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC). The Met has not contacted all the women whose cases he investigated during his 20 years as a serving officer.

The upskirting image that was sent in March 2024 to a woman we are calling Layla should have led to Arter's arrest.

Bail conditions or custody would have prevented him from taking his wife, Rebekah, to Barbados.

On 28 June, Arter rang Rebekah's relatives from the island to tell them she had died.

Rebekah had been escaping an abusive relationship in 2006 when the Met put then-Det Sgt Warren Arter in charge of investigating her former partner.

Arter pursued Rebekah, they began a relationship and he quickly moved in with her.

Her now-adult son, Elliot, says Arter initially made his mum feel "safer" but that his behaviour soon changed.

"He'd say to her: 'Get in the kitchen, make my dinner you slag. Make me a tea you [expletive] bitch,'" Elliot recalls.

Arter would openly watch pornography on his tablet while he was in the living room with her, Elliot says.

He also collected urine from Elliot, claiming he was testing it at the police lab to help the boy's promising football career - but Elliot now suspects it was an effort to hide Arter's drug use.

The inquest into Rebekah's death heard evidence that use of sedatives had become so routine in the home she shared with Arter, that a daily smart-speaker reminder announced "G o'clock" - a reference to the date-rape drug GHB.

In the years before she died, Arter had filmed and distributed videos of his wife being sexually abused. The BBC has seen some of them.

Many show her unconscious or otherwise incapacitated while Arter insults her.

"You should get raped," he says, in one video.

In another, Arter can be heard speaking to a man behind the camera, asking him to be quiet and saying "they go mad otherwise" - suggesting the video was being made for a wider audience.

His crimes were so brazen that he sent abuse videos of Rebekah unsolicited to at least four women he knew.

Two were women whose cases he had investigated - one of them was Layla.

She had met Arter in 2010 after she reported being raped. His exploitation of her continued for more than a decade, up until she reported the upskirting image - which she had deleted - to staff from the IOPC.

Both Layla, and her adult daughter who was with her when she spoke to the IOPC, say she identified the woman in the photo as Rebekah - whom she recognised from previous videos.

The IOPC says the staff member has no record or recollection of being told the identity of the woman in the photo - and it did not have the authority to investigate as Arter was no longer a police officer.

It did, however, tell the Metropolitan Police about the upskirting allegation.

It is not clear when his bosses found out about the relationship, but some of his colleagues appear to have known early on.

The BBC understands that four officers told the IOPC investigation they believed Arter had met Rebekah on a case. One said they knew Rebekah had been a victim of domestic abuse, but they refused to sign a statement.

The Met told Panorama that the IOPC's subsequent report had found that Arter's colleagues knew of his relationship with Rebekah, but did not know he had met her in the course of his duties, therefore he was not subject to any misconduct proceedings.

None of the various investigations into Arter led to criminal charges before he was arrested in 2024. On one occasion, he even received a payout after being arrested for harassment.

The IOPC has now told the BBC that of 21 possible Arter victims it had identified by 2020, it assessed he had inappropriate contact or relationships with eight of them, including Layla and Rebekah.

Panorama has, however, learned of at least one more alleged victim who says she was groomed and sexually exploited over 12 years.

Former Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Dame Vera Baird, is calling for an investigation by an outside force into all the cases Arter handled throughout his career.

"If a doctor had been found to abuse one person, they would look at all his list from start to finish.

"It's quite outrageous - there will be women living now with trauma imposed by him on them."

When Det Insp Jaysen Veeren tried to investigate Arter a decade ago, he says senior Met bosses tried to interfere with his work.

Veeren was a fast-rising officer in the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards (DPS) - which investigates police misconduct - and says he was warned he would be a "fool" to join the team because of its reputation within the force.

"The DPS is referred to as 'the rats' - you eat your own," he says.

But when, in 2016, he intercepted a Crimestoppers tip complaining about Arter's conduct with victims, he recalls telling his boss: "This is the case that I joined for."

Initially, his investigation was well resourced and he travelled to Australia to interview a woman who said Arter had sex with her after she reported being sexually assaulted as a tourist in London.

Veeren then cold-called other cases.

"We had one victim and, all of a sudden, you've got a second, third," he recalls. "It was quite obvious you're dealing with a predator."

Arter had been able to visit many of the women alone. One woman told Veeren: "He may as well have walked into my house with his [penis] out".

Veeren eventually arrested Arter and suspended him in December 2016 but Arter's phone had been wiped.

He then designed a plan to contact all the women whose cases Arter had investigated, but says he was prevented from doing so and his team encountered "interference" from senior officers outside of the DPS.

Emails seen by the BBC reveal his investigation was likened to a "witch hunt" by a detective chief inspector, who questioned its justification with the Met "haemorrhaging talent". A chief superintendent told Veeren's boss that staff felt the case was a "fishing expedition".

The two senior officers - who have since left the force - told the BBC this was not interference and said they were acting on concerns of colleagues about how the investigation was being carried out.

Veeren says he felt unable to widen his investigation and examine all of Arter's cases.

He referred his case into Arter to the IOPC in the expectation it would do so, and later reported his concerns to the watchdog as part of a wider whistleblowing complaint - alleging corruption within the DPS.

He resigned from the force in 2019 when he discovered none of his allegations would be upheld. The Met says his complaints to the IOPC had either been disproven or not corroborated.

Within hours of their first meeting, Arter asked Layla to put her head in his lap and then he stroked her hair, while a PC drove them to a sexual assault referral centre.

There, Arter was found by staff alone in the toilets with her.

A doctor was so alarmed by his behaviour that she reported concerns to the Met about his intimacy with Layla.

Layla has told us that Arter remained present while she had an internal medical examination.

The Met failed to investigate or monitor the detective's ongoing contact with Layla, who at the time was a vulnerable alcoholic.

Arter visited Layla dozens of times over the next few months, she tells us, sexually exploiting her during what he described as "therapy time".

Panorama has learned that Arter told colleagues that Layla was becoming too attached to him.

He was commended for victim care in her case - just as he had been in the domestic abuse case of his future wife, Rebekah.

Even after Arter informed Layla that the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) had declined to authorise charges in July 2010, he continued to contact her - helping her with a successful compensation claim under a government-funded scheme.

After Veeren referred his investigation to the IOPC, the watchdog described Layla as having been "groomed" by Arter.

Layla says Arter, who by this time had been suspended, was telling her what to tell investigators. She did not provide them with a statement.

Despite Layla's known vulnerability, and the evidence against Arter, it took three years for a file of evidence about his sexual misconduct to be sent to the CPS, which then declined to pursue criminal charges in 2020.

It was a further three years before Arter appeared at a misconduct hearing - and only then for drug offences.

He was finally dismissed from the Met in 2023 - have received at least £300,000 in pay while suspended. He kept his pension.

However, despite having left the force, a decision to review Arter's alleged sexual misconduct was then made.

In March 2024, IOPC staff visited Layla at home. She revealed Arter had sent her the upskirting image. By this point, she says she had begun to "wake up" to Arter's exploitation of her.

The watchdog told the Met about the illegal image - but the force failed to arrest him.

The Met told Panorama this was because of human error when using a new crime recording system.

They say they found a variety of drugs and hidden CCTV cameras that Arter had rigged up.

They also discovered photographs of Rebekah naked and bruised, involved in sexual acts, seemingly taken without her consent.

On 2 July, Elliot and Lacey drove to Bexleyheath Police Station - the same station where Arter had worked.

Staff were initially uninterested in Rebekah's death thousands of miles away, say the couple - and it was only when they mentioned Arter's name that officers became interested. "It was like chaos," Lacey says.

The family say they were told the Met was considering sending officers out to Barbados to help the investigation.

However, the BBC has been told that a senior Met boss from its Gold Command group was briefed that evening about the incident, in light of Arter's alleged offending, and a decision was taken not to send officers to the Caribbean island.

The Met told the BBC it took this decision because no allegation of criminality had been made.

Later that week, the Met visited Layla and interviewed her about Arter, where she disclosed he had raped her on one occasion and sexually assaulted her on another.

Arter flew back to London from Barbados on 9 July and was arrested at Heathrow Airport, accused of rape, voyeurism and coercive control. He took his own life in prison three days later.

Neither the Met nor the IOPC has ever released their investigation reports into Arter's sexual misconduct - despite Freedom of Information requests by the BBC.

Arter was seen as the star detective in a unit lauded for its results investigating rape and sexual assault.

But the Met has never investigated that unit's "sanction detection rates" - the proportion of reported crimes for which action was taken against suspects.

In 2009, Conservative politician James Cleverly, then a Member of the London Assembly, said the unit had achieved rates of 96%.

This is despite the figure being three times the London average and at a time when some officers were known to be systemically manipulating the recording of offences. The Met says it does not recognise the 96% figure.

If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line

Dame Vera says there seems to be many missed opportunities to stop Arter, spanning from 2006 to 2024: "There must have been other people who knew exactly what was going on."

Rebekah's family say the Met should investigate whether other men helped Arter abuse her.

When she died the Met seized electronic devices from the house she had shared with Arter. Elliot says some of those devices have not been analysed in two years.

His solicitor says a public inquiry is needed to reveal the full extent of Arter's offending.

"It's a disgrace for the Metropolitan Police, and it's also a dirty secret - one they want to keep hidden," says Sophie Naftalin.

The Met told Panorama that Arter could have been arrested sooner and it was "deeply sorry" for the harm caused to victims by his repeated exploitation of his position for sexual purposes.

It acknowledged progress with Arter's devices had been slow but said it was now being prioritised, and it encouraged anyone else who believes they were targeted to come forward.

It added that the recording of rape cases was examined nationally in 2014 - and there have been significant changes to the scrutiny of crime figures.

The IOPC says it regretted that its investigation took three years but it was a complex case involving delays out of its control. It added that the allegations were treated "extremely seriously" and resulted in referrals to the CPS.

The CPS says it thoroughly reviewed this evidence but concluded there was no realistic prospect of conviction at that time.

It says it did charge Arter with misconduct in public office before his death in 2024.

In September 2025, the UK coroner in Rebekah's case issued what is known as a prevention of future deaths report.

It said there was a risk that further deaths could occur unless action was taken.

In response, the Met said it had already taken action to improve vetting and to tackle police officers abusing their powers.

The IOPC said information had not been made available to it at the time of a specific risk to Rebekah, and that it had since strengthened its safeguarding procedures.

Elliot says he has spent the past two years trying to get answers.

"I don't think I've grieved yet", he says.

"I don't know what will happen when that day will come."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Watch: How predatory Met detective's behaviour became increasingly extreme
BreakingNewsTab.text:
BBC Panorama can reveal the Metropolitan Police missed opportunities to stop predatory detective, Warren Arter, from sexually exploiting vulnerable victims of crime, whose cases he investigated.

Warren Arter used his position to target the very women it was his job to protect, including his future wife, Rebekah, whose sexual abuse he filmed and distributed before she died in mysterious circumstances in Barbados two years ago.

A former detective inspector who began an investigation into Arter in 2016 claims senior bosses tried to interfere with his inquiry despite him finding multiple potential victims.

Arter's abuse spanned almost 20 years until his death on remand in HMP Wandsworth in 2024. The Met has not reviewed all the cases he was involved with.

The Met told the BBC it was deeply sorry - and encouraged anyone who believes they were abused by him to come forward. A spokesman said that intelligence reports it received were acted upon, but it acknowledges Arter could have been arrested sooner.

The Met also said it is working to examine his digital devices to try to identify if there are further victim-survivors or evidence of criminality.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Komyshuvakha: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after strikes that killed 57
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.

Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.

The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there have been multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.

The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged.

"Due to the threat of repeated shelling, emergency workers are constantly forced to periodically suspend work and retreat to a safe place," it added.

The DSNS said the death toll had risen to at least 72 people making it one of the deadliest single incidents since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.

International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.

Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".

Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.

Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

BreakingNewsTab.title: Cass report author says she does not support draft conversion practices bill
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she doesn't support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.

Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.

She was speaking at a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, which the government said would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.

A government spokesperson said they welcomed her comments and would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right".

Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.

This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.

There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.

When the government introduced its draft legislation, external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it, external.

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not".

She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.

But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".

Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities."

But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.

"If a young person, for example, has been sexually abused, any discussion about it is going to be incredibly triggering.

"But if you can't therapeutically work through it without any reference to it, and that's the problem," she said.

She said that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.

Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but hadn't had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.

When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.

She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]."

The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.

"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.

"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."

The committee hearings continue.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK weather: Met Office yellow warning in place as snow could disrupt rush hour travel
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Parts of northern England and southern Scotland are getting an early taste of winter with snow falling over some hills on Tuesday morning.

A Met Office yellow warning for snow is valid until 11:00 GMT with 5-15cm expected at some locations above 300-400m elevation.

Major routes like the A74(M), A66 and M62 could all have problems with transport disruption.

Some railways are also likely to be affected with longer journey times for train services.

Cold health alerts are also in place, external for northern England issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 09:00 GMT on Thursday.

A weather front is pushing north and east across the UK bringing a spell of rain to many areas. Over northern England it is encountering a reservoir of colder and drier air.

Some of the rain is evaporating in this drier air, cooling the atmosphere further by a process known as evaporative cooling - the same process involved in cooling your body down when you sweat.

Rain has turned to snow over parts of the Pennines, Cumbrian Hills and Scotland's Southern Uplands.

The snow could come down in big, wet, chunky flakes which could stick to power lines and tree branches.

The extra weight of the snow combined with wind gusts of 40-50mph over high ground could bring down tree branches and power lines, bringing an additional risk of some localised power cuts.

Some snow may accumulate down to 100m elevation or so, with around 1-5cm possible.

Any snow in these lower hills will probably be quite short-lived, turning back to rain by mid-morning in many parts, however the highest hills and mountains of Scotland and northern England could continue to see wintry weather into the afternoon.

Cold outbreaks of rain will be left across most northern areas of the UK through Tuesday afternoon with some hill fog and a chilly wind.

Meanwhile the south will have sunshine and blustery showers but it will also be milder with temperatures up to 14C.

Rain and showers will continue to impact Northern Ireland, England and Wales for the next few days.

There will still be some rain in Scotland on Wednesday but then high pressure will take over with sunnier weather returning.

This drier, sunnier weather will then push southwards across most of the UK by the end of the week with cold air returning, along with some overnight frosts and a few coastal showers.

You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Failed asylum seekers face removal without five-day notice period
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The government is to change the law so that it no longer has to give failed asylum seekers notice before they are removed from the country.

Currently, people are given five working days' notice but ministers believe this leads to last-minute appeals which delay the process.

Under the new rules, once an asylum claim fails, the Home Office would have six months in which to remove the applicant without telling them in advance.

The move was criticised by the Refugee Council which said: "Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety to people."

Imran Hussain, the director of the refugee charity, said: "The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns.

"If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer."

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood will make the change by amending the Immigration and Asylum Bill which is currently going through Parliament.

The amendment will scrap the notice requirement for those who have exhausted the asylum appeals process.

Instead, the Home Office will have the power to remove people immediately, a power that will remain in place for up to six months.

The Home Office has not said how many additional people it thinks it will be able to remove but has pointed to Denmark where the number of migrants awaiting removal more than halved over five years to under 1,000 after a similar policy was introduced.

The previous government, led by Sir Keir Starmer, had pledged to clear the asylum backlog.

In June 2026, there were 40,168 people waiting for an initial decision on asylum application claims and a further 90,341 waiting for the outcome of an appeal in the courts.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, 38% of asylum decisions led to the applicant being granted refugee status.

Forty percent of all asylum claims come from people who arrived in the UK by small boat.

The remaining 60% of claims are made by people who arrived in the country by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and subsequently applied for asylum.

Anna Turley, minister for border security and asylum, said: "We are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.

"This bill will restore order and control to the system, ensuring it is swift and fair."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital have reportedly been struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

The missiles hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges spanning the Dnipro River, Klitschko said, adding that water and power supplies had been disrupted.

Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the landmark Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea killing two people, the region's Moscow-installed governor said.

President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier warned that Moscow might launch further strikes on the country on Monday night, after Ukrainian, US and European officials held further talks aimed at ending the years-long conflict.

Those online talks, attended by US envoy Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, came after Russia said it recorded the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".

"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.

Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services have been damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.

Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October.

Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.

Separately, the Ukrainian military struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day, the region's Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram.

Traffic across the bridge had been suspended, he added.

The landmark bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014.

Russian President Vladimir Putin inaugurated the bridge to great fanfare in 2018. The severity of the latest strike on Kerch Bridge is still unclear, though it is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.

The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.

Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.

He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".

In an address on Monday evening, Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.

Zelensky said that Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will participate in negotiations with Moscow - including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the EU and Nato.

The Ukrainian president has long called for European delegates to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.

He also said that Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.

Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.

Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.

Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
