BreakingNewsTab.title: Forensic expert says his analysis of autopsy photos suggests Epstein was killed
BreakingNewsTab.text:
This article contains distressing details and references to suicide

A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.

The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.

Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.

Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.

Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.

He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings in London on Monday evening.

Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.

Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein. His research has not been peer reviewed.

He told the BBC that he believed there are signs indicating an assault on Epstein, including a deep haemorrhage to his left shoulder and injuries that appear to be consistent to being struck in the face.

Freeman said he believed the evidence was most consistent with strangulation using a ligature and then that same ligature was probably used to suspend the body from the bunk bed.

He said there appeared to be fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck, which "would be consistent with strangulation, particularly from behind. And the attempt by the victim to try to remove the ligature from the neck".

He said "the injuries and the way the body was found don't match up. There's only one remaining explanation then, and that is that the death was as a result of a homicide."

BreakingNewsTab.title: US Vice-President Vance will decide 'sometime next year' about presidential run
BreakingNewsTab.text:
US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will make a decision "sometime next year" about whether or not he will run for president in 2028.

In an interview with Fox News, Vance would not provide a timeline on making a determination, but signaled he is not in a hurry to make up his mind.

"I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year," Vance said. When pressed by host Laura Ingraham, he added: "When I make a decision, I'll be all in on whatever that decision is."

The comments came amid growing interest in Vance's next moves in the weeks since voters handed both President Donald Trump and Republicans a resounding defeat in the midterm elections.

People in Vance's orbit who have spoken to the BBC said the November elections did not change the timeline around his decision-making process for 2028. He is expected to run but allies believe he could wait several months to make a final decision.

Speculation about Vance's White House aspirations began the moment President Trump selected him as his 2024 running mate. The pick positioned Vance, who entered the White House as one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, as the most likely heir to Trump's Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.

But while serving in office, Vance has carefully avoided discussing his own political ambitions.

He kept that up during the midterms, when supporters frequently interrupted his campaign speeches to urge him to run in 2028. Vance's stock response was that Republicans needed to focus on the election at hand in November.

But with the midterms in the rearview mirror, and Republicans eager to move on from their 2026 drubbing, the next election at hand is now the 2028 presidential race.

Vance would likely jump to the top of the Republican primary field whenever he launches his bid, should he choose to run. But the contest is expected to be a competitive process with a large field of candidates.

Numerous other high-profile Republicans are rumoured to be interested in running or have said publicly that they are mulling a White House bid.

The list includes Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, outgoing Florida Governor and 2024 hopeful Ron DeSantis, and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, among others.

Trump has praised Vance and Rubio on several occasions, while also insisting that he is not sure who he will endorse in 2028 - or if he will weigh in at all.

The president's endorsement would be influential with the Maga base. But the midterms revealed widespread frustration with many of his second-term policies, complicating the path forward for potential candidates like Vance who are tied to Trump's agenda.

Vance blamed the midterm results on the war with Iran in a post-election social media post. In it, he also mapped out a plan for winning back Republican voters, which included ending the war and focusing on the economy.

The message was widely seen as a first step by Vance to distance himself from Trump ahead of a 2028 run.

In the Fox News interview, Vance reiterated his view that the war came with a "political cost", but said it has not damaged his relationship with Trump.

"There's no daylight" on the Iran war between Trump and senior administration officials including himself, Vance said.

He added that Trump would not let the conflict become a "forever war" and said the administration would not let the war, which was launched by the US and Israel in February 2026, even become "a two-year commitment".

Vance also discussed the nationwide air traffic outrage last week, which brought air travel across the US to a standstill for several hours. The vice-president called on lawmakers to fix the issue in the final weeks of the current congressional session.

He also touched on the scandal engulfing Nvidia, its former CEO Jensen Huang and its implications for US-China relations. Vance said there was still no "clarity" about the accuracy of reports that a woman with whom Huang reportedly had an affair with was indeed a Chinese spy.

"There is a lack of clarity about it. I don't know and [Trump] doesn't know whether this woman was a spy or not," Vance said.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.

"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.

Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.

Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.

Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.

In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".

He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.

"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.

He said that he is being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day, where he is allowed neither visits by his family nor access to books and television, and that this has "taken a heavy toll" on his mental health.

He also claimed he had only seen his lawyers four times over the past year.

"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he wrote.

Pakistan's parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed these claims, saying Khan is "provided with all facilities in prison, including food of his own choosing".

"[He] is currently the most well-accommodated prisoner in Pakistan," the minister told reporters.

Authorities also say Khan was taken to a government-run hospital for an eye injection a week ago, where doctors deemed him "clinically stable".

Khan, who previously captained the Pakistan national cricket team, served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 to 2022.

His arrest in May 2023 sparked large-scale, violent protests by supporters, who ransacked the corps commander's residence in Lahore, smashing chandeliers and making away with furniture, paintings, and even peacocks, among other things.

At least eight people died in the protests and the army were called in to quell the violence.

Even behind bars, Khan remains a force in Pakistani politics.

Thousands of his supporters took to the streets in early October in a dayslong march, demanding his release. Authorities later ordered a crackdown on protests and imposed a state of emergency in Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial for deaths of her three children in March 2027
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.

The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.

Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.

Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.

"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.

Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.

Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.

The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment.

FinanceTab.title: Aged 16-24 and looking for work? Use our look-up to find out which areas have the most jobs
FinanceTab.text:
If you're one of the nearly one million people aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training - otherwise known as "Neet" - then you might be wondering where to start.

Under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work, a major review aimed at cutting the number of Neets will say.

But how many jobs are there where you live and in which sectors are you most likely to find an opening?

There is no official measure of how many vacancies are suitable for young people, but across the whole economy there were 691,000 jobs available in the July to September period this year, which is the lowest number since early 2021.

The Covid pandemic led to huge swings in the number of job vacancies available as companies reacted to shutdowns and then reopened as restrictions were lifted.

Stripping out the fluctuations seen during the pandemic, the number of vacancies is now at its lowest level for 12 years.

Apprenticeships have often been a way for people to get their first taste of employment.

In England the number of people starting apprenticeships has risen in recent years, although this has been driven by an increase in those aged 25 and over after schemes for older workers were fully rolled out in 2008.

The number of people aged 24 and under starting apprenticeships in England in 2025 was 172,230, down from a peak of 291,300 in 2012.

Where you live will often have a big impact on your ability to find a job.

We have used online job adverts to help identify the number of vacancies suitable for young people in the area they live, relative to the size of the local population.

The Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) think tank used AI to help identify the jobs, which were broadly defined as roles requiring relatively low experience or education.

According to its analysis, South Oxfordshire had 387 suitable vacancies per 1,000 18 to 24-year-olds in the area - the most of any local authority. Rotherham had the least, at 53 per 1,000.

Use this tool to check out the situation in your area. The data for London is only available for the region as a whole and is not broken down by individual councils.

Even if there are jobs available in your area, you might not find one in the sector you want to work in.

The sector with the highest average number of entry-level vacancies in the year to October was teaching, with most of those jobs being for teaching assistants, learning support and cover supervisor roles, according to jobs website Adzuna.

The next largest was hospitality and catering, traditionally an area where younger people get their first experience of work.

Adzuna, a major online jobs website, includes adverts for full-time roles marked as entry-level, those asking for up to two years' experience, graduate roles, internships and apprenticeships.

Accounting and finance had the third-highest number of job openings.

FinanceTab.title: We were priced out of the market, so we bought a home with strangers
FinanceTab.text:
When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.

They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.

Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.

"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.

With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.

That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.

They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.

In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.

The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.

Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".

While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosal says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.

Gosal is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.

It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.

It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".

"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know."

Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.

While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.

"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.

Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.

In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.

For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.

Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.

Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.

"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

FinanceTab.title: Create more jobs for under-25s by cutting National Insurance, key report urges
FinanceTab.text:
National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge.

There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show.

Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest.

Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns two salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any.

Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".

She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.

"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.

Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.

"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."

The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full.

He has already unveiled some of his proposals including:

Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales

A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits.

Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.

At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270.

However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000.

This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase.

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

FinanceTab.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
FinanceTab.text:
In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.

Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”.

It has been this way since Brexit.

Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.

It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.

Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.

All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.

That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.

The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.

But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?

EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a “choice” is being made.

In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.

The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.

But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.

A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".

He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

FinanceTab.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
FinanceTab.text:
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.

Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.

It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.

The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.

"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.

"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."

Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".

She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.

"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."

Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".

She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".

Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.

The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.

The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.

Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.

This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.

He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".

A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.

The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".

He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."

Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".

The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.

However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined, external.

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.

McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.

He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.

Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

FinanceTab.title: Intel sued by investors after PC sales slump hits share price
FinanceTab.text:
Intel, the US chip giant, is being sued by its shareholders who accuse the firm of hiding the severity of a slump in its personal computer (PC) sales that caused its share price to plunge almost 29% in one day.

Billions of dollars was knocked off the value of the company after it forecast disappointing revenues ahead of its latest earnings report.

Shareholders allege that Intel made "materially false and misleading" statements that failed to disclose the slowdown in PC sales and the impact of its data centre projects, according to a proposed class action lawsuit filed in San Jose, California.

The BBC has contacted Intel for comment.

In October, Intel firm announced its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September.

That report undermined earlier suggestions from the chipmaker that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit.

Shareholders claimed the "depressed demand for PC sales" caused "a dramatic slowdown" in quarterly earnings – a drop of 9%, or about $800m - to $8.1bn.

The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders.

Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power.

As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive.

Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs.

"We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October.

Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though its share price is still up by 51% overall this year.

FinanceTab.title: Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal
FinanceTab.text:
This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you.

That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year.

Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information.

Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out.

If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January.

Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC.

Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email, external, text message, external or phone call, external claiming to be from HMRC is genuine.

"Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer.

New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October.

There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information.

To avoid being caught out, HMRC says:

it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one

it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message

it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest

In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered.

Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy.

"When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check.

"No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy."

The bank also advises doing these four things:

Pause and check, rather than being blinded by a countdown timer

Pay safely using a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger

Open an official website or app yourself rather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts

Talk to a friend, family or your bank if you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed

FinanceTab.title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?
FinanceTab.text:
It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach.

"I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.

Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.

This week, Kim Kardashian's beauty brand offered all of its customers refunds for its $148 (£110) calendar after being widely criticised on social media over the quality of its contents, with some customers likening the hair clips, scrunchies and keychains inside to things you might find down the back of a sofa.

Julia says she earns a good salary but is keen to get value for money and doesn't want to waste it on items she won't use.

"I spent £160 on a Space NK fragrance calendar last year," she says. "I got some fragrances I'd been wanting for a while for a lot less than recommended retail price, and those I didn't like I managed to sell on for a slight mark-up on what I paid."

Beauty calendars, which often cost upwards of £100 and sometimes much more, have been around for more than a decade and the marketing has grown ever more sophisticated.

High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight.

And it appears to be working. Ipsos data shows, external around 15% of all advent calendars sold are beauty ones, with people aged 18-34 particularly willing to splash out.

But in the face of that tsunami of marketing, customers seem to be getting savvier.

"I love beauty, but I rarely buy beauty advent calendars. They are pricey and often only have a few things that I actually want to try or are trending products," says Priya Raj, 30, a fashion journalist.

She thinks some are good value but, for her, the advantage is being able to try on a small scale without forking out for a full-size product.

"For me, an advent calendar - particularly a beauty one - serves the purpose of allowing me to try out different products, particularly in the lead-up to Christmas, and then I can hopefully snag a bargain in the Boxing Day sales."

Podcaster Rhea Somaiya, 28, also likes the general idea, but has a healthy scepticism around a lot of them in practice.

"I do think some brands take the consumer for granted in that they provide each day with something so menial that people are bombarded with irrelevant and cluttering items.

"And when that's the case, they certainly put me off as the excitement to open each window dwindles into irritation rather than joy."

Heather Widdows, a beauty expert and philosophy professor at Warwick University, has pointed out that while you might buy some of the products in an advent calendar individually, it's highly unlikely you'd buy all of them.

"Beauty calendars may offer you lots of products for a really good price. They can also be a bit of fun and feel sensuous.

"But it is exceptionally unlikely that you would use all the products inside them, so they're probably not worth it."

This year, Julia has spent £99 on a John Lewis fragrance calendar which she thinks is good value for money. But it doesn't mean she'll keep everything in it.

In fact she's joined a Facebook group where people trade the ones they don't want for ones they do.

"The ones I keep are already a lot cheaper per mililitre than if you bought them at retail," she says.

With additional reporting from Kris Bramwell

FinanceTab.title: Leaked Records Show Deutsche Bank Courting Russian Oligarchs
FinanceTab.text:
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.

Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.

At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.

“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”

This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.

But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.

Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

Deutsche Bank’s response to the sanctions, as well as new details about its long history with Russian clients, emerged from more than 15 million internal records, including confidential reports, emails and meeting minutes. The leaked records were obtained by the Indian author and journalist Josy Joseph and the South African journalist Khadija Sharife and were analyzed by a consortium of more than 200 journalists, including reporters for The New York Times.

The records provide a rare insider narration of Deutsche Bank’s yearslong cultivation of Russian oligarch clients. Those relationships continued even as units within the bank argued that handling the oligarchs’ finances put the bank at risk of inadvertently facilitating financial crimes.

That would be familiar turf for Deutsche. The fallout from Russia’s invasion capped a seven-year period during which Deutsche paid billions of dollars to settle claims by regulators that it had handled transactions for international bribery and money laundering, among other accusations. One of those cases involved the bank’s activities in Russia.

Even with its activities in Russia under scrutiny, Deutsche’s bankers debated how much they were obligated to tell the Justice Department about their Russian clients, records show. And bank executives initially resisted calls to exit the Russian market after the invasion. Only when competitors announced they would depart the Russian market did the bank finally pull up stakes.

Deutsche Bank, in recent written statements responding to questions for this article, said it had acted lawfully and never helped clients evade financial sanctions. “Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Deutsche Bank acted promptly to implement the rapidly evolving sanctions imposed by the relevant authorities,” the bank said.

For Russia’s politically connected ultrarich, Western financial houses like Deutsche Bank were essential. Deutsche Bank gave them the ability to do business in stable currencies and to keep their fortunes immune from Russia’s unpredictable economy and politics. Western bank accounts allowed oligarchs to buy professional sports teams and London mansions.

For years, experts have published research and given testimony before Congress showing that the Kremlin has used oligarchs as an instrument of soft power.

The newly obtained internal reports and emails capture the beginning of the end of Deutsche Bank’s long pursuit of Russian money.

Debate Over Russian Billionaires

After more than a century of an on-again-off-again presence in Russia, Deutsche Bank had become so ingrained there by 2008 that Mr. Putin spoke glowingly of the bank and personally met with Josef Ackermann, then the chief executive, in Moscow.

“The bank serves as a bridge between the Russian and German economies,” Mr. Putin said during the meeting.

Inside Deutsche Bank, some sounded warnings about these relationships — starting what would become a secret but defining pattern over the next decade and a half.

In 2014, the bank’s internal committee on reputational risk ranked its oligarch clients by the potential danger each posed to the bank’s image. At the top of the list was Mr. Deripaska, whose business interests have long intersected with the Kremlin’s and who has been called “Putin’s oligarch.”

An internal report noted that Mr. Deripaska had faced numerous allegations, including of money laundering in Spain, an ongoing tax evasion case, using the courts to “bully his competitors,” and having links to organized crime in Russia. Mr. Deripaska did not respond to questions seeking comment but previously said that he had been unfairly targeted for sanctions.

A bank division charged with insulating Deutsche from potential financial crimes raised similar concerns. Given the “frequency and seriousness of adverse information” about Mr. Deripaska, this report recommended “exiting those relationships where Deripaska is the controlling party.”

Elsewhere in the bank, in divisions focused on generating revenue, people offered a completely different take.

An internal presentation from 2015 said, “Russian billionaires contribute heavily to our success.” Those well-heeled clients were considered the “backbone of sustainable growth” for the wealth-management division, a profitable segment for the bank.

A chart from that period showed that only four countries had more households than Russia with a net worth of at least $100 million, making it “an attractive market for wealth managers.”

Around that time, Deutsche entered a long period of regulatory and law enforcement challenges. The bank paid billions of dollars to settle allegations that it had manipulated interest rates in London, handled billions of dollars in transactions for clients in countries under U.S. sanctions and contributed to the 2008 financial crisis by pushing toxic mortgages on investors.

One of those cases, the “mirror trading” scandal, focused on Deutsche’s activities in Russia. Regulators in the United States and Britain accused Deutsche of helping Russian investors launder as much as $10 billion. Deutsche paid hundreds of millions of dollars in 2017 to settle the case.

In the aftermath, Deutsche dropped some of its clients and focused instead on the wealthiest Russians, which generally meant oligarchs.

“Russia is and will continue to be one of the most attractive and significant markets for Deutsche Bank in Europe,” said a statement announcing the appointment of Borislav Ivanov as the bank’s top executive in Russia.

Risk Versus Reward

As Deutsche embraced oligarchs, ties between the United States and Russia were growing strained.

In 2018, Steven T. Mnuchin, then the U.S. treasury secretary, accused Russia’s government and its oligarchs of fostering “malign activity around the globe.” He cited Russia’s invasion of Ukraine’s Crimea region and its meddling in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. The Trump administration placed financial sanctions on seven wealthy industrialists close to Mr. Putin.

Of them, five were Deutsche Bank clients, either personally or through business affiliations, internal records show.

The list included Mr. Deripaska, who remained a client despite earlier reservations. It also named Mr. Vekselberg and the investment company he had founded, Renova Group. Mr. Ackermann, who was by then Deutsche Bank’s chairman, also sat on the board of Renova. (Mr. Vekselberg has said he was unfairly targeted for economic sanctions.)

During a meeting of the Deutsche supervisory board’s risk committee in 2019, one adviser questioned keeping the oligarchs as clients given the increasing risk, according to minutes of the meeting.

“If one of the clients turns out to be bad,” the adviser said, “the loss will be a multiple of the return.”

A document from the leaked trove shows that in September 2020, outside lawyers hired by the State of New York recommended that Deutsche Bank “strongly consider” shutting down all “operations and service related to Russia at this time.”

A lawyer representing Deutsche noted in an email to bank executives that the monitor said many other banks had already “exited Russia or significantly downsized Russian operations.”

“Is this accurate?” the lawyer asked. “Are we in line with, ahead of, or behind our peers?”

Mr. Ivanov, Deutsche Bank’s top executive in Russia, took exception, replying that a competitor was still in Russia and “5x our size” in several lines of business.

That claim cannot be verified based on public records. But Deutsche’s records show that its ties to wealthy Russians continued.

In 2018, a Deutsche Bank executive emailed a colleague to say that she had just been in Luxembourg and noticed the bank was “significantly expanding” its Russian clientele there.

She added that when she had met with Luxembourg’s financial regulators, “the first thing they mentioned was their concern related to those Russian clients.”

Deutsche had been quietly moving its oligarch accounts to its offices in Luxembourg and Switzerland, countries with strict bank-secrecy laws. That could give the bank legal cover to deny government requests for client records, though this was never stated as a motivation for the change.

Deutsche Bank, in one of its recent statements to reporters, said it concentrated its wealth-management clients in those locations, not just the Russians, following industry practices. The bank said all its Russian clients were subject to applicable vetting requirements.

In November 2020, a 172-page “Russia Strategy Review” noted that 17 Russian clients were on what was known as the U.S. Treasury Department’s “Kremlin list” of 210 senior government officials and oligarchs. Only a few accounts remained based in Frankfurt, where Deutsche Bank has its headquarters, and they were being moved. It noted Russia’s “elevated” risk for money laundering and sanctions — but also noted “the relevance and profitability of the Russian market.”

An internal review, code-named Project Oak, explored how Deutsche’s correspondent banks in Russia could pull it into problematic transactions involving wealthy clients. Yet spreadsheets attached to internal emails in 2021 showed the bank still planning to expand its oligarch clientele.

Regarding several business accounts linked to Mr. Vekselberg, the sheets noted that the bank’s anti-financial-crime division in Switzerland wanted to “exit the whole client relationship.” Employees elsewhere in the bank had concluded “that this is not possible at the moment.”

By then, Mr. Vekselberg had been under U.S. sanctions for years. His $100 million yacht had been seized by the Spanish and U.S. authorities in Mallorca. Mr. Deripaska also remained a client.

Yet again, Deutsche hung on.

In April 2021, Deutsche’s management board unanimously voted to pursue careful growth in Moscow, citing improvements to its internal controls. A draft of a report presented to the board cited the “relevance and profitability of the Russian market.”

An internal bank email said the prosecutors stressed “that the Bank will be closely scrutinized and judged on whether it is responding quickly and accurately.”

Because Deutsche Bank had moved oligarch accounts to countries with strict secrecy laws years earlier, it had legal grounds to refuse to disclose details about those clients. Deutsche “is not permitted to disclose customer data from Switzerland and Luxembourg to the D.O.J. (banking secrecy),” one specialist wrote in an email.

The bank also appears to have withheld details about companies that were less than 50 percent owned by oligarchs under sanctions, as generally allowed by a Treasury Department rule. That appears to have exempted some of Mr. Deripaska’s holdings, among others. (The bank, in its response for this article, did not address what information it provided the Justice Department.)

Prosecutors apparently accepted Deutsche’s responses. The bank said that it fulfilled its obligations under its agreement with the U.S. government. The Justice Department did not respond to requests for comment from the consortium that reported this article.

By March 2022, sentiment in Germany had swung sharply. The government provided weapons to Ukraine, agreed to European sanctions against Russia and halted its undersea gas pipeline from Russia.

On March 10, Christian Sewing, Deutsche’s chief executive, told employees that the bank would end some, but not all, of its Russian business. “We are often asked why we are not withdrawing completely from Russia,” he wrote in an email. “The answer is that this would go against our values. We have clients who cannot exit Russia overnight. And, as far as we can, we will continue to also support them, too, at this difficult time.”

That same day, as public pressure mounted, JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs said they would withdraw from Russia.

Then Mr. Sewing reversed course. The following day, Deutsche announced that it was winding down operations in the country it had long seen as important to its future.

“There won’t be any new business in Russia,” the statement said.

FinanceTab.title: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
FinanceTab.text:
The Justice and Commerce departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singaporean data center firm suspected of chip smuggling and whose former executive had an affair with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism of the Commerce Department in recent days for its failure to pursue penalties against Megaspeed, which has been under investigation for allegedly shipping advanced artificial intelligence chips into China.

The company was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe China’s Ministry of State Security recruited as an intelligence asset. Megaspeed has said that it complies with all laws and that Ms. Huang currently has no role in the company.

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist known as the entity list, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.

The announcement of a criminal investigation is extraordinary because officials do not typically comment on such matters before they are completed. The departments said that they would work together to “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

President Trump on Monday acknowledged that Mr. Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had been at odds over how hard to crack down on the loophole that has allowed China to access advanced A.I. chips through data centers in other countries.

“One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Mr. Trump said of his two cabinet secretaries, speaking to reporters on the South Lawn before leaving for a trip to Asia. “Both are acceptable, but they’re different views.”

The release said that the Commerce Department had initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, the department requested records from Nvidia on its sales to Megaspeed. Commerce officials visited Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed Ms. Huang, it said.

Following this, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The New York Times reported on Nov. 9 that the Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed was halted last fall under atypical circumstances, after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.

Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top official at the department had given him permission to reach out about the case, alarming others in the department. The incident raised questions about what Commerce officials had discussed with Nvidia, and some viewed the interaction as potentially tainting the case. The case was then transferred to the Justice Department.

The Commerce Department announcement also said that, in June 2025, Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list.

But trade records obtained by the Times from ImportGenius, a data platform, show that a subsidiary of Megaspeed’s in Malaysia called Speedmatrix continued receiving large shipments of Nvidia technology for eight months after that.

Between October 2026 and February 2026, Speedmatrix received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia A.I. technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips, which were banned from being sent to China.

Most of those shipments went to Speedmatrix through third-party manufacturers that buy chips from Nvidia and make them into servers. But in February 2026, trade records show that Nvidia International Inc. sent a $13 million shipment of electronic equipment to Speedmatrix.

Nvidia provided a similar statement to The New York Times about the “block list” last week. It said that it received permission from the Commerce Department to ship some repair parts to Megaspeed after imposing its “block.”

Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. Megaspeed advertised the relationship as recently as October, calling its Indonesian unit “a premier business partner of Nvidia.”

The Commerce Department said it had charged 17 defendants across six separate investigations over allegations of smuggling and sharply increased monetary penalties compared with those in the Biden administration.

Mr. Lutnick had also clashed in recent months with other senior officials over rules that would clamp down on data centers in Southeast Asia serving Chinese clients. The Commerce Department issued that rule Monday, but took the unusual step of saying that it had been “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council,” both agencies it had clashed with.

FinanceTab.title: Debt Problems of the Richest Countries Are Trickling Down to the Poorest
FinanceTab.text:
It’s hard to find a government these days that is not struggling with crushing public debt.

The financial problems of wealthier nations have been monopolizing the spotlight. The United States, Britain, France, Italy, China and Japan are all facing record or near-record debt levels. The fallout has been painfully visible in France, where anger at rising costs and crumbling public facilities and services helped provoke violent protests and a general strike in recent weeks.

But rich countries’ fiscal problems do not just pool at home; they trickle down to amplify the financial pressures on low and middle-income countries.

The result is that less-well off nations are borrowing more and paying more for their loans. Their combined debt surged last year to $9.4 trillion, according to a World Bank report this month.

The poorest of the poor countries fare the worst: They are facing interest rates not seen since the late 1980s.

Surging inflation pushed central banks to raise interest rates, which in turn has contributed to higher borrowing costs around the world.

“Debts that previously looked completely reasonable suddenly were carrying interest burdens that were well in excess of what a developing country can really afford to be paying,” said Christina Segal-Knowles, managing director, international policy at the Rockefeller Foundation. “That has led many countries to get in a really pernicious cycle.”

Big debts in wealthier nations are also affecting countries lower down the income latter. Bond yields — the returns paid to buyers of government debt — are surging around the world. Private investors, increasingly worried about ballooning deficits and other challenges, are demanding to be paid more for taking on the risk of lending even to wealthy countries when they fear political leaders are shirking hard financial choices.

The U.S. bond market — the world’s largest and most consequential — helps drive what happens elsewhere. U.S. Treasuries are widely considered the safest in the world. But a federal debt of more than $40 trillion, roughly 120 percent of the size of the American economy, has aroused concerns.

Mounting deficits and the administration’s policies have helped push yields on U.S. Treasuries past 5 percent, reaching levels not seen in two decades. In France, bond yields are at a 25-year high, while Japanese bond yields are trading at their highest levels in three decades.

In turn, lower and middle-income countries, whose economies are nowhere near as strong as the United States, must offer even heftier premiums to compete.

The Ivory Coast, Kenya and Nigeria, for example, have had to promise lenders annual interest rates ranging from 7.5 to more than 10 percent.

Borrowing from institutions like the International Monetary Fund has also become more expensive for all but the poorest countries. That’s because the rates offered by the fund are based on interest rates set by key central banks.

“You see how the actions of the central banks of the advanced economies determine the cost of borrowing,” said Martin Guzman, a professor at Columbia University and a former economics minister of Argentina. “Ecuador has nothing to do with the war in Ukraine or Iran, but somehow they end up paying a higher interest rate to the I.M.F.”

And the Federal Reserve and other major central banks are expected to remain under pressure to raise rates further.

The high cost of repaying existing loans and accessing new ones are constricting political leaders’ ability to govern, regardless of their ideological bent. With so much money being redirected to pay down debts, there is less and less available to pay for education, health care, pensions, infrastructure, economic development and more.

Fifty-one countries, home to 3.7 billion people, spend more on interest payments than on health care or education, according to the United Nations Trade and Development.

At the same time, foreign aid and low-interest loans from advanced economies and multilateral development banks have dried up. China, which went on a lending binge in the 2010s, is now more focused on collecting money than on handing it out.

Mavis Owusu-Gyamfi, president and chief executive of the African Center for Economic Transformation, underscored the need for joint action.

“China is a big player in this game and until we can reach a consensus with them,” she said, “every single debt negotiation is going to be in bits and pieces and is going to take a long time.”

What’s particularly frustrating is that money designated to promote growth is being siphoned off. Countries that receive lower-interest loans from international financial institutions like the World Bank or regional development banks end up using some of that money to repay private lenders instead of investing in businesses or creating jobs.

Many emerging economies in deep debt have avoided default, but not necessarily because they have achieved financial stability. Instead, they have prioritized repaying their loans.

“It means defaulting on development rather than on debts,” Mr. Guzman said.

FinanceTab.title: Appeals Court Weighs Pentagon’s Media Restrictions
FinanceTab.text:
A federal appeals court in Washington on Monday heard arguments in litigation about a set of media restrictions put in place by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, including a rule that all reporters who visit the Pentagon must be accompanied by an escort.

The New York Times had sued to overturn the policy on First Amendment grounds. The three-judge panel pressed both sides with tough questions.

Under Mr. Hegseth, the Defense Department has moved repeatedly to curtail journalists’ access to the military complex, often arguing that the restrictions are necessary to protect national security. Beginning in October 2025, the agency said it could strip reporters of their press passes for soliciting or publishing classified information and some unclassified information. Instead of complying with the rules, journalists from mainstream outlets surrendered their press credentials.

The Times sued over the initial policy in December 2025, arguing that the policy violated journalists’ First Amendment rights to gather newsworthy information without the prospect of punishment. In March, Judge Paul Friedman of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled in favor of The Times.

Days later, however, the Pentagon released a new set of rules, including the escort requirement. The Times challenged the revised policy in a second lawsuit, and, again, Judge Friedman ruled in its favor, scolding the Pentagon for “such a blatant attempt to circumvent a lawful order of the court.”

The Pentagon appealed both of the judge’s rulings.

At Monday’s hearing, the appeals court panel considered the escort requirement and other elements of the Pentagon’s revised media policies from March, which sought to clarify the October 2025 rules.

Judge Judith W. Rogers, a member of the panel who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, questioned the government’s approach to the Pentagon press corps.

“It’s as though you didn’t like violin music, so the orchestra leader said, ‘Get out of my orchestra.’” And then after the court ordered the violinist back to work, said Judge Rogers, “you tie his hands.”

The more “apt” analogy, argued Jack Starcher, who represented the Defense Department, is where “the violinist is put back in the orchestra in a different seat or in a seat that he considers less favorable to him.”

“He’s in the practice room,” quipped Judge Rogers.

Judge Patricia Millett, who was nominated by President Barack Obama, asked the government about a rule that said that the Pentagon could bar a reporter if it had “any doubt” about whether a journalist might pose a security risk. She said that standard would be hard to challenge.

Mr. Starcher said that it’s “hard to answer questions about what these provisions will actually look like in effect because these provisions have never been allowed to go into effect.”

“So they’re not clear,” responded Judge Millett.

Judge Millett also grilled Theodore J. Boutrous, a First Amendment lawyer representing The Times. Does the First Amendment, asked Judge Millett, really protect a reporter who goes into the Pentagon and seeks to pry classified information from an employee that the journalist knows is not authorized to share it?

“You’re saying the First Amendment allows you to do that?” asked the judge.

“I am saying that, your honor. That is our system,” responded Mr. Boutrous.

Judge Millett also asked whether The Times could demonstrate adverse consequences from the escort rule, which has been in place for several months. Mr. Boutrous responded that declarations from numerous journalists show that the Pentagon’s rules pose a “significant burden” on reporters.

The other judge on the panel is Karen LeCraft Henderson, a nominee of George H.W. Bush. It is unclear when the panel will issue a ruling in the case.

The Times’s suit is one of several pieces of litigation between media companies and the federal government or Mr. Trump in recent years. In September, CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued over their expulsion from the White House grounds; though they secured a judge’s order restoring their press credentials, they remain barred from rotations in the pool that covers President Trump in confined spaces.

The Associated Press, furthermore, sued the White House after it was barred from pool coverage. That case is also before the federal appeals court in Washington. Mr. Trump has sued major news outlets — including The Times, The Wall Street Journal and television news networks — over their coverage.

SportsTab.title: Scotland: What's the story with Sebastien Pocognoli, is it now time to go?
SportsTab.text:
A few short months ago, Craig Mulholland, the Scottish FA's chief football officer, and Ian Maxwell, the association's chief executive, spoke about the worldwide search for a new Scotland head coach.

The data, the metrics, the cosmic input from the analytics company whose input was received at Hampden as if written on tablets of stone.

The process all pointed to Sebastien Pocognoli being their guy. They paraded him around Hampden, told everybody that loads of clubs were on his tail but that they won the chase.

They may, or may not, have mentioned the word 'coup' but that was certainly what their body language was telling you.

For coup, read boo, the sound surely reverberating around the Tartan Army right now after Monday's 4-0 defeat by Switzerland.

Some nonsense has been written about Pocognoli being on twice the salary that Steve Clarke was on, but whatever they're paying him, there's no value in it so far.

Money is a factor here. Clarke's three qualifications brought a rich bounty into the SFA's coffers, many millions even after deductions. That cash gave the association a little more opportunity to do some of the things they want to do in grassroots football.

A world where Scotland miss out on major championships and the financial windfalls that come with qualification is not a place they want to revisit. The next Euros looks like a gimme - almost harder not to qualify than qualify - but the sense of drift in this team is alarming and can't go on much longer.

Mulholland, Maxwell and let's throw SFA president Mike Mulraney into the mix, should be feeling mightily nervous.

Most people understood that Pocognoli needed time, but implicit in that understanding was a need to see something developing under him, a burgeoning style of play, some positives here and there, a few signs that even though things might not be great today or tomorrow, they're inching in the right direction.

There's been none of that. Decent players look lost. Pocognoli's system has made Scotland a disjointed soft touch. Structural discipline collapses too often. Players charge forward and leave space in behind. He wants hard pressing and maximum intensity, but his players don't look capable of providing it.

In six games they have scored five goals - two from the penalty spot. Promises of jam tomorrow are not cutting it. People can see a team on the slide.

In Switzerland, there was a drubbing that piles the heat on the Belgian, on the people who appointed him and on the players, too.

If the chaos on the field wasn't a bad enough look for Pocognoli, then some of the words said in the wake of this objectionable 4-0 pummelling to a Switzerland B side playing in third gear only made things worse.

Andy Robertson, on the night he became Scotland's most capped player in history, delivered a damning riff that sounded strongly like a commentary on this coaching regime and this set of players.

In his stead, John McGinn did much the same thing. "You don't get time" was the gist. Who doesn't get time?

Robertson and McGinn didn't lay it on the line, but their thoughts resembled distress flares. These Scotland players can be overhyped, but they are better than some of the nonsense they dished up in St Gallen.

More than one former Scotland international reckoned they saw players not exactly busting a gut out there. These guys know the tell-tale signs.

Some private conversations between the SFA hierarchy and the senior operators in this team need to take place. What were they suggesting in the post-match? What are they really thinking?

An honesty session behind closed doors needs to take place long before the qualification campaign for the next Euros begins in March.

Not many fans were buying what he was selling. Listening to some of his players, you doubted that they were buying it either.

After the home loss to Slovenia, Robertson said his team had been "out-played" and "out-fought." There were some other comments made after the desperately stodgy 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday. On Monday, it cranked up another level.

McGinn was asked if he felt Scotland were on the right path. "Impossible for me to say yes," he replied. It was hard to listen to what the players were trying to say and conclude that everybody's on the same page in this set-up.

Intransigence is not a good characteristic for any manager. In recent times we've seen a few bosses at big clubs who were wedded to their principles. Russell Martin and Wilfried Nancy didn't last long at Rangers and Celtic.

To repeat Robertson's line, you don't get time.

Clarke had an instinctive understanding of that and pragmatism was his way of taking his team forward, difficult yard by difficult yard. Rigid idealism is not a sensible way to operate, but Pocognoli has gone down that road in his first six games.

It's a dead-end down there. He needs to turn back and find another way while he still can. If he still can.
