SportsTab.title: Mario Balotelli: Why always him? The rise and fall of the Italian striker
SportsTab.text:
Maverick. Loose cannon. Unmanageable.

Mario Balotelli heard it all.

Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines.

Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, which came just days after a firework was set off in his own bathroom, causing a house fire.

The 36-year-old is still playing, now in the United Arab Emirates first division with Al-Ittifaq alongside his biological brother, Enock Barwuah.

Here, BBC Sport looks at a career that has included 13 clubs, six countries - and an assist for arguably the most famous goal in Premier League history.

Typical of his unconventional footballing life, Balotelli's career did not begin in an elite club's academy.

Instead, by his mid-teens he was turning out for Italian third-tier side Lumezzane, close to the family home in Concesio.

A trial at Barcelona did not lead to a long-term stay, and instead he was picked up by Inter Milan in 2006.

It was at Inter that Balotelli first came across his great mentor - Roberto Mancini.

The relationship between the two has been likened to that of a father and son. Under the Italian coach's tutelage, Balotelli flourished.

Aged 17, Balotelli helped Inter win the 2007-08 Serie A title and reach the Coppa Italia final, memorably scoring twice against Juventus to send his side into the semi-finals.

Life changed for Balotelli with the arrival of Jose Mourinho in the weeks after that campaign ended.

There would be disagreements, disciplinary action and accusations that Balotelli's attitude was not up to scratch. Mourinho said Balotelli was "unmanageable" and described one performance as "close to a zero rating".

The relationship with Mourinho was fractious - a rare occasion when the Special One was confounded by a player.

Balotelli still won three Serie A titles and one Champions League with Inter, but his reputation as a supposed loose cannon was already beginning to overshadow his feats as a player.

Logic dictated that Balotelli's next step should be to reunite with mentor Mancini. That happened in August 2010 when the 20-year-old joined Manchester City.

Mancini set out to show that the unpredictable ways of Balotelli could be harnessed for the team's good, aiming to get more out of him than Mourinho could.

A hardline stance on discipline often appeared to soften when Mancini dealt with Balotelli, who by spring 2011 had garnered a reputation in England as a fantastic footballer who could not stay away from controversy.

Having already been sent off twice for City and been involved in a car crash - not in his famous camouflage Bentley but an Audi R8 - the striker threw a dart at a youth-team player, an act that showed a level of immaturity.

After helping City to win the FA Cup in 2011, ending their 35-year major trophy drought, Balotelli came under scrutiny after attempting a backheel trick shot when through on goal during a pre-season friendly against LA Galaxy.

Mancini swiftly hooked him, later questioning his mentality by saying: "If you are serious, you can play 90 minutes. If not, you can come and sit by me on the bench."

Sometimes the audacity paid off - like the famous shoulder goal and subsequent nonchalant celebration against Norwich.

On other occasions, not so much.

In October 2011, emergency services attended his Cheshire home to deal with a firework lit in his bathroom. Balotelli said a friend had been responsible.

BBC Sport reported at the time that four firefighters used two hose reel water jets to douse the flames, with a large fan deployed to clear smoke.

Days later he was in the spotlight for the right reasons as he scored City's opener in a 6-1 win over Manchester United, celebrating with the 'Why always me?' T-shirt.

There were other stories - that he had given a homeless person £1,000, that he had turned up to a young boy's school to confront the headmaster about the child being bullied, that he drove around Manchester handing out presents while dressed as Santa.

True? Perhaps only Balotelli knows and he has often denied such rumours. But such was his reputation at the time that the stories became plausible.

A chant City fans coined made reference to his ironic allergy to grass - which kept him out of a Europa League match in 2011 - and driving around Moss Side with "a wallet full of cash".

On the pitch, Balotelli was sent off against Arsenal in April 2012 in what, at the time, seemed like a season-defining moment that could end Manchester City's title bid.

But one month later he assisted Sergio Aguero's last-gasp goal against Queens Park Rangers that gave City a first Premier League title. It was his only Premier League assist that season.

Micah Richards, who was a team-mate and friend to Balotelli at City, said: "He was crazy in a good way. He was brilliant to have around the squad - a cult hero not just for the nonsense he did off the field but on it as well.

"The best thing about him is he's a lovely guy - he's not arrogant or how the papers try to perceive him, he's just a bit mad."

But did the moments of brilliance make the "nonsense" worth it?

Despite once insisting his patience with Balotelli was "limitless", Mancini ultimately had a rethink.

The final straw came in January 2013 when the pair had an argument at the training ground. Balotelli left for AC Milan later that month.

Mancini said: "He is not a bad guy, and a fantastic player, but I'm very sorry for him as he continues to lose his talent and his quality. I don't have any words for his behaviour.

"I hope for him he can understand he is in a bad way for his future."

Affection remained on both sides, but the relationship had become too fraught.

"Once upon a time, Mario did genuinely believe he was one of the best players in the world," said Nedum Onuoha, another former City team-mate.

"There are lots of stories about him from his time at City, but the one I remember is at our old training ground in Carrington when someone was talking about Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, and Mario said he was as good as them - and he was deadly serious.

"It obviously hasn't worked out that way, but he still has done so much more with his career than most players could even dream of."

Yet that tournament proved to be the peak of Balotelli's international career.

Italy's national team took a downward turn, and so too did his club career. By 2015, Balotelli had more or less became an Azzurri afterthought.

While Balotelli enjoyed some big moments in an Italy shirt, he did not always feel the love reciprocated from his country of birth.

Before Euro 2012 he threatened to leave the pitch if he was subjected to racist abuse and spoke openly about the vitriol he suffered while playing for Inter.

In fact, racist abuse has followed Balotelli throughout his career and he has commendably refused to tolerate it.

Born Mario Barwuah in Palermo to Ghanaian parents, Balotelli was placed into foster care aged three.

Initially, he stayed with his foster parents - Silvia and Francesco Balotelli - in Brescia during the week, then returned to his biological parents at weekends. He was eventually fostered on a full-time basis and took on the Balotelli surname.

Balotelli identifies with both parts of his heritage - Ghana and Italy - and he struggled to reconcile his love for a nation with the people who aimed verbal abuse his way.

The good times were all too brief: 36 caps and 14 goals has been his tally since 2018. He wanted more and has often made it known.

Onuoha said: "Playing for his country was always so important to him and that's another really positive thing about him, that he had that drive and ambition."

Was it that Liverpool move that sent Balotelli's career spiralling into freefall?

Spells in Nice, Marseille, Brescia and Monza followed - each to varying degrees of success but never with a feeling of stability.

Then came Turkish club Adana Demirspor, Swiss outfit Sion and Italian side Genoa. He spent no more than one season at a time with any of these clubs, although he did return to Demirspor for a second stint.

And so to the present day, with Balotelli aged 36 and plying his trade in the UAE.

It is easy to wonder what might have been had Balotelli stayed in Manchester, had he managed to settle enough to entirely fulfil his potential.

But, after so much media attention and a career that has spanned more continents and leagues than most, it is perhaps also understandable that Balotelli has settled on fulfilment through simply playing the game he loves with his brother.

"Playing with a family member like he is will give him that happiness," said Onuoha.

"And yes, it is not Serie A, La Liga or the Premier League, but Mario is on a field sharing it with his brother - for him that will mean everything.

"At this point there aren't many people that would hold much against him. I think when he was younger, some people would.

"But now I think it is more a case of almost allowing him this happiness, and enjoying seeing him finish off the last days of his career in a place that makes him happy.

"So many people end their careers on a sour note, but for him he is going to be ending it doing exactly what he wants to do."
SportsTab.description: Maverick. Loose cannon. Unmanageable. Mario Balotelli heard it all. Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines. Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt...

SportsTab.title: Emmanuel Oyebadejo: Scouted as a spectator, now on brink of NFL
SportsTab.text:
When medical student Emmanuel Oyebadejo went to watch his friend's American football game, he had no idea he would end up being scouted himself for a sport he had never even played.

He wasn't even interested in it. In fact, while still at school in Manchester he'd delivered a speech titled 'I have a dream' in which he outlined plans to do "very well in basketball, return from the NBA and be the prime minister of the United Kingdom".

But now, four years later, he is being tipped to become the first Briton to be a first-round pick in the NFL Draft.

It is a rapid rise for the 22-year-old, who had to learn the game from scratch and win over his parents who "begged" him not to play and instead focus on his medical studies.

His biggest challenge at the start, though, was finding a pair of boots big enough for his size 16 feet.

It was 6ft 6in Oyebadejo's physique that had caught the eye of the coaching staff at Exeter Demons when he was a spectator for his friend's university game that was taking place at the club's home ground, The Crumb.

"I was talking to one of the other coaches, Jack Mullins, and we sort of turned around [and thought] 'that guy's freaking huge! We should go talk to him'," Lydon Ward-Best, one of the Demons' coaches, tells BBC Sport.

Oyebadejo had been a talented basketball player, playing for Manchester Magic - one of England's top junior clubs - from the age of 11 to 18. But by the time he was at the University of Exeter he was no longer playing competitively.

Lydon Ward-Best persuaded him to give a new sport a go.

"He started coming to training and just had the most ridiculous intro to American football I think I've ever seen," the coach adds.

A straight-A pupil, who had also learned the piano, guitar and drums while studying medicine, Oyebadejo had always been a quick learner.

"I always say that American football is kind of like violent chess," says Mullins, the Demons' current head coach.

"[Emmanuel] got the violent bit pretty quickly. He was fine at that - 'I am much bigger than you, watch me go'.

"The chess bit took a little longer because there's all these things that you have to think about."

But as Ward-Best puts it, "he's not just a big sort of jock athlete, he's a smart guy. He is so dedicated and disciplined with everything."

Oyebadejo played for the Demons at the end of the 2022-23 season, before the team went unbeaten in his first full season, 2023-24. When back home he also played for the Manchester Titans and helped them win the Britbowl in September 2023.

By December 2023, he decided he wanted to take things further. Could he make it in the United States? Would college teams be interested if he sent them videos of his highlights?

Coach Ward-Best told Oyebadejo it would be "tough", adding: "You know the percentages are not on your side here, but you are 6ft 6in and 280 pounds (20 stone), so you've got a better chance than most.

"I wanted to be realistic with him," he adds. "But I said I'd do whatever I could to help get him out there."

Emmanuel's father Oladini says he thought it was a "joke" and that he did not support him playing this "dangerous" game, explaining: "He had never played this game before. He'd only done it for a few months, so why would anybody from America want him?"

But they did.

There was interest from several colleges and Oyebadejo ended up at Jacksonville State, where he would study biology and play under legendary college coach Rich Rodriguez, having managed to win his parents round thanks to the influence of an uncle who lived in Dallas and understood the sport.

His first season was hit by injury but, despite coming up against players who have played American football since they were young children, his second was a big success.

As a defensive end, Oyebadejo's job is to get past the offensive linemen trying to block him and tackle the ball carrier or claim a sack - when a defensive player tackles the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.

He recorded 4.5 sacks, forced two fumbles and had 41 total tackles during the 2025 season.

Now the big college teams were paying attention.

College football is America's most passionate sporting pastime. While the NFL plays on Sundays, the college game dominates Saturdays during the autumn months.

And Oyebadejo transferred to the University of Florida to play for one of college football's biggest teams in the most prestigious conference, the Southeastern (SEC).

The Florida Gators are three-time national champions, have about 50 former players currently in the NFL and get home crowds of 90,000 at 'The Swamp'.

Oyebadejo was undaunted as he burst on to the scene. He had 2.5 sacks in a win at rivals Auburn in September and followed that up by impressing in big wins over Mississippi and Texas, the latter in front of 103,989 people.

After barely being on the radar of NFL scouts at the start of the season, Oyebadejo's form has propelled him into contention to be an early-round draft pick in 2027.

NFL teams do not have youth systems or academies. Almost all players have come through the US college system and they are recruited via the NFL Draft when they graduate.

One of the biggest events in the American sporting calendar, the NFL Draft takes place over three days in April, with the 32 teams taking turns to select players across seven rounds.

First-round picks in April will be guaranteed a rookie contract of at least $19.1m (£14.4m) and they are often fast-tracked into starting roles. The contract values decrease in a sliding scale so, for example, a third-round pick (top 96) will be guaranteed $7.3m (£5.5m).

Among the latest prospects, ESPN's veteran draft analyst Mel Kiper has ranked Oyebadejo as the fifth-best edge rusher (defensive end). That is regarded as the sport's second-most important position behind quarterback - and therefore the second-best paid in the NFL.

The reason is that Oyebadejo has everything needed to be a starting defensive end in the NFL. Firstly, his height and weight are ideally suited for the grappling battle required in what is known as 'the trenches'.

He has very long arms (7ft wingspan), perfect for winning a wrestling match against the kind of enormous opponent he faces, and unusually for a man as big as him, he's extremely quick. That's the money-making trait.

Although he now weighs about 300lbs (more than 21 stone), it is believed he has a remarkable body-fat percentage of about 12%. All his measurables are seen as ideal for a defensive end, if not better.

There are simply very few people with Oyebadejo's physical talent, and given the fast-tracked nature of his rise in American football, he does not look as raw as you might expect.

"He's British and has only played the sport for three [full] seasons," says his mentor and former coach Ward-Best. "You'd therefore think he must be very green, but he doesn't look that way.

"The physical qualities are clearly there but he's worked a lot on mastering aspects of the position as well."

Menelik Watson, also from Manchester, holds the record for being the highest-drafted British player. He was the 42nd pick in 2013 and spent six years in the NFL, earning a total of $16.4m (£13.7m).

London-born Osi Umenyiora, the 56th pick in 2003, enjoyed an illustrious 12-year career - winning two Super Bowls with the New York Giants.

"I have spoken to Osi, he's a really cool guy," says Oyebadejo, who is also of Nigerian heritage.

"To be a first-round pick out of the UK, it would be amazing. It would do so much for the American football community back home."

Oyebadejo impressed again in an upset win at Kentucky on Saturday and has 4.5 sacks with two regular-season games left. Florida could then play in a 'bowl' game, an end-of-season exhibition.

After that, Oyebadejo is expected to participate in a physical-testing event called the 'scouting combine', where he will be assessed by representatives of all 32 teams in March.

The draft then begins in Washington DC on 27 April, and if Oyebadejo hears his name called, he will complete an unlikely journey and make his now fully supportive parents very proud.

"It's mad," says Ward-Best. "I've been doing this for 20 years and I've never seen anything like this. We almost have to pinch ourselves."

Oyebadejo has stayed in touch with his former coaches in Exeter. The Demons hold watch parties for Florida games and there is a real sense of pride over where his journey began.

"It was just complete chance that he wanted to wander up to The Crumb and watch a game, just being there for his mate," says coach Mullins.

"If those things didn't happen, we wouldn't be having this conversation. He would be four years into his medical degree."

SportsTab.title: Grand Slam of Darts: Luke Littler lands triple-bull checkout, as Gerwyn Price benefits from maths error
SportsTab.text:
Gerwyn Price and Luke Littler both made it through to the Grand Slam of Darts knockout stage on a night featuring a bizarre maths error and a sensational triple-bull checkout.

Littler suffered a 5-4 defeat by Dutchman Niels Zonneveld but claimed the three legs he required to progress from the group stage.

The 19-year-old, egged on by the crowd at the Aldersley venue in Wolverhampton, improbably landed three darts on the bullseye to produce a remarkable 150 checkout and level the match at 4-4, only to lose the deciding leg.

Price, meanwhile, claimed a 5-2 victory over Sebastian Bialecki - although he was the beneficiary of an unusual mathematical mistake.

The Welshman was 2-1 up against Poland's Bialecki and required 135 to win the fourth leg.

Price's first dart hit treble 19, leaving him with 78, but he asked referee Charlie Corstorphine what he had left to score and was incorrectly told 88.

In good faith, Price promptly threw treble 16 and then double 20 to win the leg, having scored 145 - which should have bust him.

"A rare scoring error was made by the referee in the fourth leg of the match between Gerwyn Price and Sebastian Bialecki," organisers the PDC told BBC Sport in a statement.

"Under Darts Regulation Authority (DRA) rule 6.4, as the error was not corrected before the next leg began, the leg score stands as announced."

Price said he was unaware of the miscalculation until it was flagged up to him before he walked into a post-match news conference.

"I hit the first treble and I asked 'what have I got left?' and he said 88, so I threw treble 16 and double top, then he said 'game shot'," said fourth seed Price.

"I'm glad I didn't know, because it probably would have played on my mind."

SportsTab.title: Ireland v South Africa: 'Is that not match fixing?' - Rassie Erasmus questions officiating
SportsTab.text:
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has predicted Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast will not face a ban after being cited, and questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?"

Prendergast became the first player to be cited under World Rugby's new regulations for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji and could be banned for Saturday's Nations Championship match.

Speaking at a media conference on Monday, Erasmus said the 23-year-old's tackle was "terrible", but he believes Prendergast will be free to play against the Springboks in Dublin because of a "technicality".

The 54-year-old also added that he thought it was an "immediate red card" when he saw the tackle occur in the first half of Ireland's 43-15 win, but it was not penalised in-game by referee Angus Gardner or by the television match official Mike Adamson.

"I must say the right words now. We are in the northern hemisphere. I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play," Erasmus said when asked about Prendergast being cited.

When he was asked to elaborate on what he meant by a "technicality", Erasmus said that, while he is "not a legal guy", "it never seems to go our way".

"I'm not saying anybody's doing anything wrong. I'm just not expecting him to get [suspended] - I think he'll play on Saturday," Erasmus said.

World Rugby has been approached for comment by BBC Sport over Erasmus' comments.

Erasmus, who said "I swear I'm not moaning", also pointed to how Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong avoided punishment for an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster in October.

Last year, South Africa prop Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban for a similar offence and missed November's matches for the Springboks.

"Tadhg got off free for the same thing Jan-Hendrik did. I don't want to go into details because I'm not a legal person, but from a South African point of view, that hurt," added Erasmus.

"I'm telling you now for any neutral - and I'm not saying the neutrals are right - but for anybody that looks at that situation on exactly the same two things that happened, one guy's word was taken, and another guy's word was not taken.

"One guy got nine weeks. He didn't play for the Springboks, and the other guy played the next weekend. That's all I'm saying."

In 2021, when he was South Africa's director of rugby, Erasmus was banned for two months by World Rugby for an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' first-Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions.

World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".

The following year, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.

Erasmus said there had been a meeting with World Rugby over the implementation of new laws surrounding the hip-drop and knee-drop tackle for November's internationals, which Ireland and France coaches didn't attend.

Hip and knee-drop tackles are when the tackling player drops their body weight on the legs of the ball carrier, and Fiji captain Peceli Yato was eventually forced off with an injury against Ireland after he initially continued following Prendergast's tackle.

South Africa head into this weekend's game in Dublin off the back of a narrow 21-19 defeat by France at the Stade de France on Saturday.

After saying he would get in trouble if he showed video evidence, Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles by French players were not penalised by match referee Andrea Piardi or the TMO Matteo Liperini in Paris - 11 of which he thought were penalties and three which he felt should have been yellow cards.

Erasmus said his comments were "not an accusation" about the officials, and questioned World Rugby's prerogative to limit interruptions from the TMO.

"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.

"Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game if you see this injury that happened there, a knee-drop tackle happened there, and it's been decided that knee-drop tackles are out?"

Erasmus said his players spoke to Piardi and the officials about the number of knee-drop tackles, and he doubled down on his views over the lack of intervention from the TMO.

"They happened 17 in our games. Not one was penalised even," Erasmus said.

"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.

"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

SportsTab.title: Thomas Frank: How former Spurs boss could restore his reputation and save Crystal Palace
SportsTab.text:
"When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank in June.

That time is now after the Dane was confirmed as the new manager of Crystal Palace, who are two points and a goal difference deficit away from safety at the bottom of the Premier League.

Former boss Pierre Sage was sacked last week after just 16 league and cup games.

The role offers Frank an opportunity to rebuild his reputation after he was sacked by Tottenham in February after eight months.

Frank described it as "an honour" to be "in charge of this fantastic football club" as Palace announced his arrival on a deal running to June 2029.

"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League," Frank told Palace's website.

"I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."

Palace chairman Steve Parish said Frank was the "perfect fit for our club".

But how big is the challenge at Selhurst Park that awaits the man who made his name at Brentford?

"It's going to be a bit of a shock for Thomas Frank," former West Ham and England goalkeeper Rob Green tells BBC Sport.

"He had his success at Brentford - a very well-run club where players are brought in with a lot of thinking and planning to take over the players they sell for profit.

"That doesn't happen at Crystal Palace.

"They lose players and then have a mad scramble to get players in. They have a team that has been decimated by sales and not replaced by the same quality.

"Thomas Frank needs to find something within that team that builds and garners the belief that means that they can compete in the Premier League, because it feels a long way short of that right now."

Will Frank prove the right fit for Palace and haul the Eagles out of the relegation zone?

Since getting the sack at Tottenham after 26 league games last season, Frank has been out of management longer than he was in charge of Spurs.

In the summer he released a statement in which he said "there have been conversations and opportunities" to return to management, but that he had "decided not to rush into the next role".

Frank's name was heavily linked with Palace before they went for a head coach with no Premier League experience to replace Oliver Glasner - the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Conference League title and the Community Shield before moving to Nottingham Forest.

"Palace had one of the best managers they have had, if not forever, silverware coming across the doorstep. Look at what they achieved last season and instead of building on that, they dismantled a team," said former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

"They have regressed."

Frank once described managing as being on a "hamster wheel" and a "crazy circus"., external

Palace confirmed his coaching staff will include current assistant manager Paddy McCarthy and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy, who previously worked with him at Brentford.

Justin Cochrane, who is part of Thomas Tuchel's England staff, is set to join.

Palace are also in the process of approaching Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who would join as assistant first-team coach.

It is understood Frank would like to take Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, though the north London club are determined to keep the Swede.

Denmark fitness coach Chris Haslam, who worked with Frank at Tottenham, is another potential member of Palace's new coaching set-up.

A trip to Coventry City awaits Palace on Saturday.

So why does Frank feel now is the right moment to return to management at a club propping up the table?

Frank, who was part of BBC Sport's World Cup punditry team during the summer, will be coming into the job refreshed and with renewed energy and enthusiasm following several months out of the game.

Between his appointment as Brentford boss in October 2018 and the sack at Tottenham earlier this year, he managed without a break for seven years and four months.

Spending the past few months away from Premier League pressure has allowed Frank, in his own words, to "study, observe and learn from other leaders both within sport and beyond".

Will his positivity and passion rub off on a Palace team who have lost seven times in 10 top-flight matches?

Thomas Frank has a lot of work to do as Crystal Palace have undoubtedly been the worst team in the Premier League so far this season, ranking bottom not just in points (seven) but also goal difference (-14) and expected goal difference (-8.1).

It's the defence where Frank will have to focus most of his attention. Not only have Palace conceded the most goals (24) but they've also faced the most shots (189) and have the worst expected goals against (xGA) figure in the league (21.9).

Their attack has actually not been too bad. While only Hull have taken fewer shots, the Eagles have created really good chances and have perhaps been unlucky not to score a few more goals given the opportunities they've had.

SportsTab.title: Wales v Portugal: Portugal without Cristiano Ronaldo face a post-Gareth Bale Wales
SportsTab.text:
Portugal are just one match into life after Cristiano Ronaldo, a footballing titan whose 23-year international career transformed the game in his homeland.

On Tuesday, they visit Wales, who are nearly four years into a similar adjustment after the retirement of their own icon, Gareth Bale.

History might suggest these two teams belong to different echelons of the sport. But in terms of individual players defining entire nations, Wales and Portugal share a profound connection.

Their records only tell half the story. Ronaldo and Bale scored more goals and won more caps than any other man to represent Portugal or Wales. In Ronaldo's case, more than any other man in the world.

What the two represented for their respective countries went beyond their remarkable statistics, though.

Ronaldo led Portugal to their first title at Euro 2016, beating Bale's Wales in a semi-final and ending a momentous Welsh journey in what was their first appearance at a major tournament for 58 years.

Both players gave their countries countless memorable moments, and not only on the international stage.

Former Real Madrid team-mates, Ronaldo and Bale won four and five Champions Leagues respectively, a combined five La Liga titles and a plethora of other team and individual accolades.

Whenever they held trophies aloft, you could bet they would be carrying, or often wearing, the national flags of Portugal and Wales – global ambassadors.

"You're losing an icon of the national team," says Wales captain Ben Davies, Bale's former team-mate and part of the Welsh defence which faced Ronaldo in what proved to be his final international appearance two months ago.

"But it's an opportunity for other players to stand up and try to take that limelight. We've had boys who've really stepped up in that time after we lost probably Wales' greatest player.

"Ronaldo's a big loss but football moves on."

As secure as their legendary status might be, there are telling differences between the two.

When Bale announced his retirement aged 33 in January 2023, he did so because he acknowledged his once otherworldly powers were fading and he felt Wales needed to plan for the future.

Reserved by nature, Bale could not avoid an outpouring of adulation, but he tried to depart as quietly as he could.

By contrast, Ronaldo's exit earlier this month was messy, acrimonious and, according to some, long overdue for the 41-year-old.

He walked out of a Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start a Nations League match against Denmark, resulting in a £215 fine and 30-day suspension.

Without knowing beforehand that the Wales game earlier that month would be his last, Ronaldo did not get the send-off he would have wanted.

"I'm grateful that we got to see the longevity of a true great who's had one of the biggest impacts in football," says Wales head coach Craig Bellamy.

"He's left a mark on football that will live forever. I'm grateful I got to see him and I'm grateful I got to coach against him."

Glittering and record-breaking as Ronaldo's international career undoubtedly was, the final few years were somewhat strained.

At this summer's World Cup and other recent tournaments, his star was clearly on the wane, prompting some to question whether Portugal might be better off without him.

Some of their underwhelming performances with Ronaldo leading the attack may have backed up that view, but supporters of the five-time Ballon d'Or winner could point to Portugal's first game since his retirement – Saturday's 4-1 home defeat by Denmark – as a riposte.

"You were all having a go at him for playing and then as soon as he retires then suddenly it's all hell breaks loose," Bellamy adds.

"He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We are all going to miss him.

"Portugal will be completely fine. Portugal are able to leave players who cost £80m to £100m out of their squad. They can pick 30, 40 players and be ridiculous. Before that you had Figo, you had Rui Costa, before that you had Eusebio.

"The game will move on, but I always feel we should celebrate him."

Bellamy makes an important point, highlighting arguably the biggest distinction between Portugal's prospects after Ronaldo's retirement and the task Wales have faced since Bale's departure.

Portugal's squad is among the best in the world, littered with world-class talent in every position, a true embarrassment of riches. As Bellamy says, they will be fine.

The current Wales squad, meanwhile, features four League One players and one on loan in the National League.

The two teams are in the same Nations League group but worlds apart.

While Bale was part of a wider golden generation, the fact that Wales have always had to rely on thinner resources than their rivals only added to the sense of wonder that they could produce this phenomenon.

The likes of Harry Wilson have taken their game to new levels since Bale's retirement but, as the Leeds United playmaker himself said earlier this year, nobody can replace Wales' greatest.

Nobody will claim to be able to replace Ronaldo either. In Portugal, he has an almost religious following.

In pure footballing terms, though, they have more than enough to fill the void. Four of this year's Ballon d'Or nominees were Portuguese.

The reigning Nations League champions travel to Cardiff on Tuesday shorn of an all-time great but still blessed with a galaxy of stars.

"Does it [Ronaldo's retirement] change how we approach the game? It doesn't, because it's just the level of quality you're up against," Bellamy says.

"They still have about 15 Champions League winners in the squad.

"They were fine before him, then they had a brilliant moment with him, and they'll be brilliant after it as well."

SportsTab.title: Wales v Australia: Five key areas for Steve Tandy's side to back up All Blacks win
SportsTab.text:
As the dust settles on Wales' historic victory over New Zealand, work is under way to secure another major scalp.

Steve Tandy's side ensured their place in history by ending the 73-year wait for a win against the All Blacks.

Now they must back up what many are describing as the one of the greatest results in Welsh rugby history by beating Australia in Cardiff on Saturday.

Wales have won just one of their past five meetings with the Wallabies and are without a victory over them in Cardiff since 2021.

But victory would complete only their second ever clean sweep of autumn internationals following the statement win on Saturday.

"[Beating the All Blacks] wasn't even by fluke, that's the nicest thing," former Wales centre Tom Shanklin told the Scrum V podcast.

"It wasn't like there were two or three cards for New Zealand. Wales did it the hard way and deserved to win."

So what must Wales get right this week on the final weekend of the Nations Championship group stage?

Not often can rugby results be genuinely described as historic, but the euphoria surrounding a first win over New Zealand since 1953 can easily be excused.

Players and fans broke down in tears at the final whistle on Saturday, as much in surprise as relief. The wait to beat the All Blacks again has been agonising.

But Tandy now has the immensely tough challenge of lifting his players once again to somewhere near that emotional and physical peak.

"Wales need to have that same mindset and belief, that's the biggest task after that emotional high," said Shanklin.

"I think they will be alright. Games like this can change your career [and] Australia are there for the taking."

Former Wales fly-half James Hook added: "We were in a world of pain after going out of the [2007] World Cup, then we go to Twickenham and win when nobody believed we could. The week after against Scotland, we just didn't think we could lose - and we didn't.

"These boys will go into that game against Australia and will feel that they can't lose and hopefully, the crowd gives them the ovation they deserve."

Victory over New Zealand was inspired by Wales' epic defensive stand.

Beauden Barrett said it felt like New Zealand were running into a red brick wall as Wales racked up a remarkable 346 tackles.

Tandy brought in ex-Glasgow defence coach Peter Murchie during the summer to work alongside contact specialist Dan Lydiate and the move is paying off.

Shanklin believes the mind-set and physical comitment was reminiscent of the demands of Grand Slam-winning defence coach Shaun Edwards.

"There was the drive and mindset to keep them out and make big hits," he said.

"There was one player on the floor and the rest in the defensive line.

"They got back up every single time, nobody was slow. Every time the All Blacks looked up there was a red wall."

Australia may have lost their past four Tests and have just one victory in six - albeit against world champions South Africa - but they have regularly been free-scoring against Wales, including eight tries on their most recent trip to Cardiff in 2024.

Wales' attack finally sparked as they racked up a record try tally against New Zealand in Cardiff.

Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit crossed as Wales scored five tries against the All Blacks for the first time.

After labouring against Japan, Anscombe said New Zealand looked "shell-shocked" by the accuracy and physicality of the Welsh attack.

Shanklin added: "Wales nailed it. We saw them play with attacking options, width, tempo and quick ball.

"The attack looked slick with options everywhere. Nobody was running on their own and there was a tip-on either inside or outside. Wales made the right decisions and were clever in how they attacked."

As well as fly-half, Tandy faces a selection dilemma in his back-row having rung changes between the Tests against Japan and New Zealand.

Taine Basham hugely impressed against the All Blacks, as did Taine Plumtree off the bench, but Aaron Wainwright could be available following an ankle injury.

And while Alex Mann has been a regular first-choice at number six, his Cardiff team-mate James Botham took his place with a man of the match display on Saturday.

"Sometimes you have guys that play well at regional level [but] when they play at the Test arena they go up a couple of notches. Botham is like that," said Anscombe.

"He was physical, made tackles and got through so much work. He has to be a regular in the back-row, even though they are blessed with options."

Steve Tandy's side ensured their place in history by ending the 73-year wait for a win against the All Blacks. Now they must back up what many are describing as the one of the greatest results in Welsh...

SportsTab.title: Cristiano Ronaldo: Portugal boss Jorge Jesus responds to criticism from Ronaldo's mother
SportsTab.text:
Jorge Jesus has responded to claims by Cristiano Ronaldo's mother, Dolores Aveiro, that her son had been "deceived" by the Portugal manager.

Ronaldo, 41, retired from international football on 5 November, ending a career with his country during which he won 234 caps and scored 146 goals.

But his retirement also came less than a month after he had been given a 30-day suspension and fined £215 for walking out of the Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start the Nations League match against Denmark.

Portugal played their first game since Ronaldo's announcement against the Danes on Saturday, losing 4-1 at home.

While attending a Sporting event on Monday, Aveiro was asked about Ronaldo's national team retirement, and said:, external "Of course he was sad.

"They deceived him. And I'm sad, too. The defeat [against Denmark] was well-deserved. I was actually glad."

Before Portugal's Nations League game against Wales in Cardiff on Tuesday (19:45 GMT), Jesus was asked for his thoughts on Aveiro's comments.

"Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo's mother?" he said.

"She is a lady I greatly respect - she suffered a lot to raise her children."

Asked if the debate about Ronaldo's international retirement would end, Jesus added: "I don't know when it's going to stop.

"If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer."

SportsTab.title: Has James Trafford replaced Jordan Pickford as England No 1?
SportsTab.text:
It was some night for James Trafford.

As he was mobbed by his England team-mates for a late double save that secured a memorable 3-2 win against world champions Spain, the debate that followed about who the country's number one is was inevitable.

The Leeds keeper was given his chance to show England boss Thomas Tuchel what he could do again - and he absolutely took it.

On his fifth England cap the 24-year-old enjoyed a magnificent performance in Madrid as his side handed the hosts their first loss in 43 matches.

Trafford made four key saves in the final 12 minutes of the game, including an incredible double stop to first deny a Lamine Yamal curler and then dive again to his right to keep out Fermin Lopez from close range.

Last week Tuchel had made it clear that Everton goalkeeper Jordan Pickford was his number one.

But after full-time in Spain Tuchel told ITV Sport "there's no number one" and Trafford had "a brilliant match".

So, following his performance on Sunday night, is Trafford now likely to oust Pickford as England's go-to goalkeeper?

Despite being just 24 years old Trafford has already been England's most expensive goalkeeper by transfer fee... twice.

Trafford returned to his boyhood Manchester City from Burnley for a £31m fee in 2025 and then left the Etihad for Leeds for £45m this summer - having been limited to being Pep Guardiola's 'cup goalkeeper'.

Given the downturn in form of their current goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, many City fans may well be wishing Trafford had stayed. Their loss is Leeds' - and maybe England's - gain.

At Leeds he has found his form and this season ranks first among the 52 goalkeepers who have played at least 10 games in Europe's big five leagues by save percentage (81.4%).

He has made five appearances for England, all of them in 2026, and has rotated with Pickford across the Three Lions' five matches since the World Cup.

Pickford has started against Czech Republic and Croatia twice whereas Trafford has played against Czech Republic and started both England's matches with Spain, home and away.

After England's win in Madrid, which was the first time Spain had lost in the city in 39 years, Trafford's double-save was praised by his Three Lions team-mate Declan Rice.

"Everything happened so quick so for him to make two in the space of two seconds is massive," he told ITV. "A massive night for him."

Spain manager Luis de la Fuente agreed. He said: "We did generate some chances but England's goalkeeper has produced a fantastic performance and stopped two or three potential goals in the last 10 or 15 minutes."

After the double-save several England players ran over to celebrate with Trafford.

And on Tuchel's decision to rotate between his two keepers former Manchester United captain Roy Keane told ITV: "I think it's smart management.

"This is the perfect time for Trafford to come in, against top players, and show what he's capable of doing."

Social media has been full of the 'England number one' debate since, with many suggesting this was a moment that marked the changing of the guard.

Could Tuchel really now not start with Trafford for England's Nations League quarter-finals? Only time will tell.

What about Pickford though? England's undisputed first choice for almost 10 years has rarely let his country down.

The 32-year-old has won 94 caps for England since making his debut in a 0-0 draw with Germany in 2017 and during his time as number one England have reached two World Cup semi-finals and two Euros finals.

According to Opta stats, Pickford has only made two errors leading to goals across his England career, with 46 clean sheets and a 74.3% save ratio.

And since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.

"We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that," said former England number one goalkeeper Paul Robinson to BBC Sport before England's win against Spain,

"It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period.

"This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much.

"I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis any time soon, irrespective of the next selection."

This isn't a debate that is going away any time soon. But having two goalkeepers genuinely competing for that number one shirt can only be to England's benefit.

SportsTab.title: Sebastien Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Andy Robertson
SportsTab.text:
Angry captain Andy Robertson says Scotland do not have time to turn things around after a brutal 4-0 defeat by Switzerland consigned them to a third-place finish in their Nations League group.

Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli - appointed as Steve Clarke's successor in August - has consistently stressed the need for patience as he tries to implement a more attack-minded style.

However, the Belgian has won just two of his first six matches in charge, both against North Macedonia, and conceded 10 goals in that time.

They collapsed worryingly easily in St Gallen against a much-changed Swiss outfit on Monday after a promising start, Bologna midfielder Lewis Ferguson putting through his own goal and early intensity gave way to indecision.

The Swiss struck twice in the early minutes of the second half to make it 3-0 and Zeki Amdouni made it four late on.

"First half, I thought we were in the game, we lost a stupid goal, but I thought we had chances and could have been 2-1 at half time," a frustrated Robertson said, on the night he surpassed Kenny Dalglish as his country's most capped men's player.

"By the time you get to 50 minutes and you're 3-0 down, that can't happen in international football.

"It is a really tough night for us. I don't think you've got time in international football, you have to do it.

"These supporters who travel everywhere, are they going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden who are going to be critical and rightly so? No.

"We don't have time, the players do not have time, we have got to step up.

"We have a long break now to March, which is not a good thing, and it is going to be a tough one to swallow."

This was meant to be a special occasion for Robertson, but it was usurped by the debate over Pocognoli's future.

Just six games into his tenure, there are serious questions being asked over whether the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco coach is capable of delivering on his promise of making Scotland easier on the eye, while delivering positive results.

Tottenham Hotspur left-back Robertson was not the only player to deliver a scathing assessment.

When asked if Scotland were on the right path, John McGinn replied: "Well, obviously the trajectory of the results means it's impossible for me to say yes."

Fellow midfielder Billy Gilmour added: "As a team we know we need to show passion and fight. We've not quite done that tonight."

Supporters are already frustrated at Pocognoli's 3-5-2 formation as they see wingers sidelined or - in the case of Ben Gannon-Doak - shoehorned into an unfamiliar wing-back role.

One man familiar with the difficulties of being the Scotland manager is former boss Craig Levein, who believes the Belgian needs to take a leaf out of his predecessor's book.

"Pocognoli is picking up where Clarke left off," Levein said on BBC Scotland. "In that situation, you need to get off to a good start. That's what the players are looking for - that you're going to make them better.

"I'd be thinking 'we need to stop losing goals'. We haven't got a potent threat, so how do we get results? As Steve recognised, you need to be hard to beat."

In contrast to his deflated players, Pocognoli put on a brave face post-match and insists he sees positive signs after his first two camps.

"The score is heavy with the 4-0, but I don't think it's a reflection of the game," he said.

"We played a good first half, we created chances, we were dominant in some moments, and we faced Switzerland with different shapes and adapted well from the first minute. We conceded from maybe one of the first chances they had.

"At the end, it's a bad feeling, the score, but I think that the players try to do their best and create moments that we want to see."

Again Pocognoli called for patience and the time which Robertson says Scotland do not have.

"The more we have games together, the more we will try to fix these things," the head coach said. "We have a lot of good response from this camp and it's good for the future as well."

But whatever Pocognoli's selling, former Scotland winger Pat Nevin isn't buying.

"If I'm ever in trouble and I need a PR man, I'm getting him because he's absolutely good at it," he said on Sportsound.

"He's certainly a glass-half-full person. You can talk away any moment and say it's just a moment, but it's four moments, five moments, six moments.

"A really horrible thing in that situation is that if I am running the SFA, I'd be asking the players what they think and just saying 'tell us the truth... are you backing us?'

"If a couple of the main ones say 'we're not sure of the decision-making' then I think it's got to that stage."

Fraser: Utter shambles. Embarassing. How can players who play for so called "big" clubs look like they've never seen a football before when they put on a Scotland shirt?

Matt: Six games. Six poor results. Our ranking will tank. And all Clarke's good work will be undone. It's time to admit Mulholland got it wrong. Sometimes you don't need data and metrics to see the simple solution. Poco no more.

Shirleyanne: All these comments about how rubbish we are I would like to know if they are the same people who when we play well are getting in touch praising the team?? The manager needs time, the players need time too.. Yes it's not been great but come on give them a chance and get behind them instead of moaning..

Grant: Pocognoli is the new Russell Martin, talks a good game but is actually clueless and too stubborn to admit his tactics are dire. I did say be careful what you wish for when the gaffer quit in June and this will only end one way so might as well get it done well before March. Someone should call Steve Clarke.

Brett: When you have limited resources like Scotland, you have to utilise them to good effect - take a look at what Michael O'Neil is doing with Northern Ireland, he is getting results. And you can say that Scotland has a better pool of players to choose from than Northern Ireland does, so...

SportsTab.title: Shoe Prices Hit a Record High Amid Inflation and Increased Tariffs
SportsTab.text:
Americans are paying more for sneakers, boots and high heels, another sign of how inflationary pressures have spread to nearly every aspect of consumer spending.

The war in Iran has driven up the price of oil, which has raised the price of gas, groceries and other goods transported by ship and truck. The surge in energy prices has affected the footwear industry too, as the some of the materials used to make shoes are synthetic byproducts of petroleum and thus more expensive.

Increased production costs combined with higher tariffs on products manufactured in Asia pushed shoe prices up 2.1 percent in the United States in October to their highest level, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The figure from the same period last year is missing because of a federal shutdown.

Still, there’s little sign that prices will fall soon. “We expect to see record footwear prices for the full year,” said Gary Raines, the chief economist of the Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America, a trade association. “That is strongly influenced by those average duties prepared on footwear that have been trending higher over the last year and a half.”

Historically, footwear price inflation has averaged 0.35 percent every six months from 2000 through June 2026. In the first half of this year, it rose 2.3 percent, the biggest semiannual jump since pandemic-related supply chain problems upended shoe production four years ago.

Shoe companies have worked to keep prices steady on their most popular items, such as Nike Air Force 1s and Crocs classic clogs, but have turned to incremental price increases on less vital products.

But even some of the most prominent shoe lines have increased prices. This year, Deckers Brands, the owner of Ugg, raised the price of its classic sheepskin boot 2.6 percent to $195 and said its Hoka running shoe brand would see some price increases this fall.

Footwear executives have said throughout the year that their businesses have been pinched by higher costs of materials such as leather and textiles. Andrew Rees, the chief executive of Crocs, said in April that its resin clogs, made from a proprietary foam, faced cost pressure as disruptions from the war in Iran sent oil prices skyrocketing.

Top executives from Adidas, Steve Madden and Birkenstock have each said that higher freight costs, brought on by those high oil prices, have affected their businesses.

Birkenstock said it had raised some prices as it pushed costs on to consumers. Ivica Krolo, the chief financial officer of Birkenstock, suggested on a conference call with analysts and investors in August that price-conscious shoppers traded down to the brand’s cheaper offerings.

“Our pricing decisions are made with the goal of passing through inflation and protecting gross margin,” Mr. Krolo said. “Something that we do very consistently.”

American consumers have kept spending this year even as they struggle with higher costs of living, but they are starting to pull back. In September, U.S. retail sales rose just 0.8 percent, down from a 1.3 percent gain in the previous month. Shoppers are expected to prioritize value in their purchases as retailers enter the crucial holiday season.

“The consumer keeps showing up,” Matt Priest, the chief executive of the Footwear Distributors group, said of the retail landscape. “But we don’t know how long that will last.”

Since President Trump returned to the White House, many of the world’s largest footwear brands, including Nike, Adidas, Skechers, Puma and Crocs, have pushed the administration to lower tariffs and alleviate pressure on their margins. In a letter sent to Mr. Trump last year, they said that the new tariffs presented an “existential threat” to the industry and asked him to consider an exemption.

The industry got a reprieve in February when the Supreme Court ruled that Mr. Trump was not authorized to unilaterally impose tariffs, but new duties under a different statute took effect in July.

The world’s largest shoe exporters are China, India, Vietnam, Indonesia and Bangladesh, and the United States has assigned each of these countries additional tariffs on top of duties already applied to footwear.

The Trump administration also left footwear out of its latest rounds of tariff exclusions, which have included categories such as wind turbines and commercial aircraft.

In July, the American Apparel and Footwear Association, an industry trade group with members that include Adidas and Steve Madden, sent a letter to the U.S. trade representative’s office that requested a list of footwear and other goods be considered for lower tariff treatment.

“Tariff relief broadly benefits U.S. workers in our industry,” Beth Hughes, the group’s vice president of trade and customs policy, wrote in the letter. “U.S. consumers stand to benefit since tariff costs ultimately make their way to the final consumer.”

TechnologyTab.title: New Zealand tricks and annual leave - the lengths fans are going to for GTA 6
TechnologyTab.text:
After 13 years of waiting, some GTA 6 fans are taking extra steps to play the game - from booking time off work, buying a console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.

Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates, external GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn (£894m) from 12 million pre-orders - although Rockstar has not confirmed this.

Despite the option to preload the 212GB game, Jennifer Holmes, chief executive of the London Internet Exchange, said several UK internet providers including BT and Virgin Media had "increased capacity in anticipation of higher demand" ahead of launch.

But for some fans, simply having the game ready to play is not enough.

Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.

When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding, external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.

Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing , externaltaking several days off to play.

GTA 6 is no exception, but it appears to characteristically be taking things to a whole new level.

For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.

It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.

According to the HR firm, one person put "new GTA is coming out! I will be spending a week on the sofa in my pants!" as the reason for their leave request, while another said: "play the new GTA - I've waited a billion years".

A third said in their request: "GTA Release - I'll put my notice in if this is denied."

The company added it had no way of tracking if the requests had actually been approved by employers.

Some places have even decided to lean into the trend by offering incentives around the game – including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.

It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.

"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.

"There are 130 soldiers eligible within the battalion, and 20 have selected this incentive as part of their reenlistment," she said at the time.

Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.

Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.

This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.

According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.

Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.

"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.

"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.

It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.

But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.

GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither has Sony nor Microsoft.

Louise Wooldridge from analyst firm Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".

Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.

Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.

"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.

A PS5 now costs from £520, while the more powerful PS5 Pro is nearly £790.

Despite the hefty price tag, for some the temptation to join the community in playing what many have called the biggest game launch of the year, if not decade, has been too great.

Reddit posts and videos, such as one by US YouTuber isoish, external, show fans buying consoles specifically to play the game.

"So, the only game I'm going to have on here is GTA," the content creator said in the video.

"The whole PS5 is for GTA 6."

After more than a decade of waiting, it seems some fans are determined not to waste a single minute of GTA 6's release - no matter what the cost or extra effort.

TechnologyTab.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack
TechnologyTab.text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.

In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.

Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".

Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.

But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.

TechnologyTab.title: Nvidia dismisses campaign to bring back Jensen Huang as Trump backs effort
TechnologyTab.text:
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.

Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.

But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.

The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.

Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.

The "Stand with Jensen" campaign claims to have been launched by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, all demanding the return of the former chief executive.

They expressed concerns the firm's co-founder "was removed without meaningful due process".

Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back.

Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of the affair but resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.

The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times, external, though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on the report.

The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House.

Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".

Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.

The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Trump administration on Monday also issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres, which have been allegedly used as a way for Chinese firms to gain access to advanced chips to train AI models.

The move comes ahead of a meeting this week between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, whose countries are locked in a race to lead AI development.

The interim rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to prevent them from being illegally diverted to China.

The measure is designed to ensure existing restrictions on sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the Department of Commerce said.

Huang has been a vocal advocate for easing chip export restrictions on China, arguing that broad access to global markets is crucial for the competitiveness of the US.

He said in 2025 that the market for AI chips in China would eventually reach $50bn - a sum Huang said "is like Boeing - not a plane - the entire company".

In 2025, Nvidia won an approval to sell some advanced AI chips in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.

The ex-Nvidia boss' affair with Alice Huang, the former director of a Singaporean data centre firm called Megaspeed, has raised the level of scrutiny over deals abroad.

The small South East Asian business hub has been a draw for companies all around the world, many of which have set up headquarters in Singapore.

Major US firms like Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have set up offices in the business-friendly country, alongside Chinese companies like TikTok-owner ByteDance and Tencent.

But Singapore's openness to business has also made it the ideal address to place orders for restricted advanced semiconductors.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the chip giant earns.

But notably, only 2% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, which acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external

"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."

Fellow tech boss Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, sidestepped the question of Huang returning to Nvidia at a conference, saying: "I don't think I know enough to answer that question."

But Altman, who himself was reinstated to his job after being fired back in 2023, said Huang was a "hero of mine".

Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.

Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.

In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".

Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.

For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk...

TechnologyTab.title: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
TechnologyTab.text:
Thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, have reported trouble accessing services.

Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch and noted the impacts may have affected other banks. It added the issue was "temporary" and not "systemic" or "cyber-related".

Problems appeared to be easing for many customers by early Monday evening.

The issue comes after a string of unrelated technical problems, including a massive Microsoft outage, a network failure that grounded all US flights, and United Airlines reporting a "widespread system outage".

Problems started on Monday afternoon. There were almost 5,000 reports of problems with Chase Bank's services, according to the Downdetector website.

Clients reported issues accessing their online accounts, viewing balances and performing transactions, like bank transfers and wire transfers, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

A Chase Bank customer in Texas told the outlet that he could not deposit a check at a Dallas branch on Monday, reporting that he was told his transaction could not be completed. He said a bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" but did not provide additional details.

Chase Bank told its customers that "some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete" but they still had "access to their accounts and funds".

The bank, a subsidiary of JP Morgan Chase, serves more than 86m customers at 5,000 branches across the US, as well as 7.4m small businesses, according to the company's webpage. It is also the top credit card issuer in the US.

The exact nature of the bug was unclear. The BBC has contacted Chase Bank.

Bank of America customers had issues at ATMs and using mobile banking services online, while US Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app, CBS reported.

Customers using another institution, US Bank, also reported issues transferring funds and Wells Fargo customers said they had problems signing into their accounts, getting account balances and making transactions.

US Bank said some its systems were not directly affected but clients using the Zelle, a digital payment platform, received error messages saying their payments could not be sent.

Zelle has said its service is "operating as it should" and issues at other banks could be affecting payments.

Customers also reported issues with Truist, PNC and Capital One but all these companies told the BBC they have not been impacted.

As of 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), Chase, Bank of America and US Bank had seen a fall in the number of reported outages.

Just as the banking issue affected US customers on Monday, United Airlines confirmed a "widespread system outage", which it described as "a technology issue affecting departing flights".

That issue resolved within a few hours.

The Chicago-based airline did not say what is believed to have caused the issue, but a spokesperson said it is not related to cybersecurity.

The issue did not appear to be affecting any other airlines.

The United issue is separate from the one that hit the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), but comes as other industries report different outages around the US.

On Friday, the FAA issued a rare nationwide a ground stop, halting all US air travel due to a telecommunication and network upgrade issues.

The halt lasted just over four hours, but the knock-on effect continues to snarl US air travel.

Additional reporting by Max Matza.
